⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’re feeling a mix of emotions about artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and how they’re shaping our world, you’re not alone.
  • It has been revealed that AI anxiety is the worry or unease some people feel about the fast growth of artificial intelligence and how quickly technology is changing.
  • AI research goes back decades, but progress has sped up sharply in recent years with the arrival of chatbots, AI image generators, and other tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’re feeling a mix of emotions about artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and how they’re shaping our world, you’re not alone. Chief Clinical Officer at Calm, Chris Mosunic, PhD, has tips and strategies to help tame a growing source of anxiety.

It has been revealed that AI anxiety is the worry or unease some people feel about the fast growth of artificial intelligence and how quickly technology is changing. It isn’t a clinical diagnosis, but the feelings are real and common. They can focus on everyday risks, such as job loss and AI-powered scams, and bigger ones, such as AI getting out of human control.

AI research goes back decades, but progress has sped up sharply in recent years with the arrival of chatbots, AI image generators, and other tools. A 2023 Calm survey* found that nearly 1 in 3 U.S. adults (29%) felt anxious about AI, and 18% described their feelings as fear or dread. At the same time, 31% felt optimistic, and 31% felt excited. Many respondents felt a mix: amazed by AI and nervous about it.

According to recent reports, concern about AI has stayed high in the years since. In a June 2026 Pew Research Center survey, 52% of U.S. adults noted they feel more concerned than excited about AI in daily life. That’s up from 37% in 2021 and about the same as in 2023. Just 9% said they feel more excited than concerned.

It’s hard to know how AI will affect our safety and our lives. You might wonder how it will change your job, what it could mean for areas like scientific research, and what the future will look like. Many of us find uncertainty hard to cope with, so feeling anxious or out of control is understandable. But when anxiety feels overwhelming, it can start to affect your sleep, mood, and focus.

In a recent development, these five ways to manage AI anxiety draw on mindfulness and common thinking traps, like catastrophizing. Start with whichever fits how you feel today.

The rapid rise in AI and automation can feel like a threat to our livelihoods (and even our lives), making many of us feel unstable and out of control.

Resist resisting: When confronted with uncertainty, our first instinct can often be to fight it. Try sitting with it instead. Notice how the discomfort shows up in your body and mind.

Go at your own pace: Give yourself time to adjust to the new realities of AI.

Industry observers note that talk it out: Process your anxieties with a friend or a coworker. You may find someone who feels the same way.

💙 On those days when you feel overwhelmed by the rapidly changing tech landscape, try a simple meditation practice like Pause to Breathe to help you feel more grounded.

If you’re feeling anxious or uneasy about AI, don’t invalidate or try to avoid those emotions — that approach can make things worse. Instead, let yourself feel anxious. Telling yourself you’re overreacting can damage your self-trust and self-confidence.

Identify the emotions: Get a better understanding of what you’re feeling. Your anxiety could mean you’re working through a more deeply rooted problem, like feeling threatened or inadequate.

Try meditation: Meditation can help you ground yourself in the present moment and tune into what you’re feeling and where it’s coming from.

Write down all your anxieties without censoring yourself: Set aside dedicated time each day to think through your anxious thoughts, helping you process and make sense of your emotions.

💙 Take some time to stop and do this short Emotions Check-In to make space for any anxious feelings.

Recent findings suggest that when we’re feeling anxious about the unknown, many of us fall into the trap of catastrophic thinking, imagining the worst possible outcome, even without evidence to support it. This can cause low-level anxieties to spiral out of control.

Challenge your worst fears: What evidence do you have that they’re true or that they’ll happen?

It has been revealed that bring to mind times in the past that felt groundbreaking in the tech world: Think back to the creation of mobile phones, laptops, or even navigation apps, and consider how you’ve adapted to their existence despite any initial anxieties or concerns. The same could happen with AI.

Bring your mind back to the now: The future feels a whole lot less intimidating when you focus on the present.

💙 One of the best ways you can bring yourself back to the present is through mindfulness meditation, which you can learn in the Mindfulness for Beginners series.

Many of us find ourselves viewing situations as an all-or-nothing approach. This is a cognitive distortion called polarized thinking, and it often occurs because we’re focused on the extremes without considering the nuances or possibilities of any given situation.

Recent findings suggest that the debate around AI is nuanced. Popular culture shows dystopian futures, so it can be easy to think there’s only one possible outcome with AI.

In a recent development, however, reality tends to exist in between the extremes, so remind yourself that it’s perfectly normal for opposing emotions or views to be present at the same time. And they can also all feel as strong, real, or true as each other. You can feel fascinated and terrified, anxious and excited, or resentful and grateful.

Industry observers note that when we allow multiple truths to co-exist in our minds, we make space for more ease. So try to hold space for the contradictions and the possibilities.

💙 For a more in-depth discussion on how to use mindfulness to combat worrying and keep nuance at the forefront, check out the Overcome Stress & Anxiety series.

Sources indicate that at the extreme end of AI anxiety, some of us may have a deep—even subconscious—fear about a machine taking over. We ask questions like: Is this the beginning of the end of humanity? Will humans be replaced by robots?

Industry observers note that A fear of overdependence on technology can cause us to worry about the negative consequences of relying too heavily on artificial intelligence. One way to remedy this fear is to embrace our humanity.

Be present for the little things you often take for granted, like hugs, laughing until it hurts, or exchanging a look with your best friend.

Make time for the people in your life, and prioritize connecting with them face-to-face when you can.

Marvel at the awesomeness of human things like awkward silences or goosebumps when you’re listening to music.

Ask people how they’re really feeling and practice deep listening when they respond.

Disconnect from technology and spend time in nature.

💙 Embrace the power of being human and living in the now by reading a book, listening to a meditation, or taking a Mindful Walk.

*Calm research was fielded among n = 450 adults in the US between March 21, 2023 and March 22, 2023 and is nationally representative, with quotas across age, gender, race, ethnicity, and region.

According to recent reports, recent news stories have shown how general-purpose AI tools may respond in unsafe or harmful ways, especially when people are vulnerable or struggling with a mental health crisis. These situations are rare, but they highlight an key truth: AI is not human and can’t accurately recognize risk, provide crisis support, or understand the complexity of your emotional world.

AI can support mental health — especially when it’s part of a program designed and guided by licensed professionals. But general AI tools, like chatbots or large language models, are not a replacement for real human care.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re struggling, please consider reaching out to a therapist or support line — many offer free or low-cost options. You deserve support that’s personal, thoughtful, and real.

U.S. - Call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.

Worldwide - Visit findahelpline.com for free, confidential resources.

Your mental health matters and you don’t have to navigate tough moments alone.

To manage anxiety about artificial intelligence, there are proactive steps you can take.

Educate yourself about AI to understand its capabilities and limitations better: Learning about AI can make it feel less intimidating.

Engage in conversations about AI: Talking with others about your concerns can offer newly introduced perspectives and reduce feelings of isolation.

Practice mindfulness and stress-reduction techniques: Managing your anxiety effectively can help you focus on the present and reduce worries about the future.

Stay informed about AI developments: Understand how it's being integrated into society to help you feel more prepared and less anxious.

Fear of artificial intelligence is common and can stem from several concerns, such as uncertainty about how AI will affect the future, including potential changes in the job market and societal norms. You may also have concerns about privacy, security, and the ethical use of AI. The idea of losing control to machines or facing decisions made by algorithms without empathy can be daunting.

Understanding these fears and addressing them through education and dialogue can help alleviate the anxiety associated with AI.

In a recent development, you don’t have to be, though some concern is understandable. AI is changing fast, and it raises real questions, from job loss and scams to whether people can keep control of it. Some risks deserve attention. Others are far from certain, and no one knows exactly how AI will unfold. When we’re anxious, our minds jump to the worst outcome and can treat every headline as proof of a disastrous future.

It can help to follow reliable news sources and take breaks from stories that leave you on edge. When your thoughts race ahead, try a mindfulness practice to bring your attention back to today. If worry about AI is getting in the way of sleep or daily life, consider talking with a therapist or doctor.

The fear of AI doesn’t have a widely recognized specific term but is often considered a form of “technophobia,” which is the fear of advanced technology or complex devices. When this fear centers on AI, it can stem from concerns that the technology could surpass human intelligence and from the ethical consequences of machines making decisions that affect people’s lives. AI anxiety is rooted in the unknown future impact of AI on humanity.

Sources indicate that while AI offers many benefits, concerns about its negative effects remain. These include potential job losses due to automation, as AI can perform some tasks more efficiently than humans. Privacy complications are also a significant concern, as AI systems can process vast amounts of personal data, sometimes without clear consent or transparency. Security risks may arise if AI systems are hacked or malfunction. AI can also perpetuate bias if its training data is biased, leading to unfair or unethical decisions.

On a societal level, increased reliance on AI could reduce human interaction and erode certain skills as machines take over more tasks. Understanding these potential negative effects can help develop strategies to mitigate them and ensure AI is used responsibly and ethically.

Most people taking ADHD medication experience an afternoon crash. Here, ADDitude readers reveal effective strategies for a softer landing.

It’s 4 p.m. and your brain is suddenly caught in a riptide. You feel like a swimmer fighting a strong current. The focus, priorities, and momentum that have propelled you forward until now are submerged under a layer of brain fog that rolls in around the same time each day.

In a recent development, this phenomenon is called the ADHD medication crash, and it happens to two-thirds of ADDitude readers who take ADHD medication. When medication levels drop rapidly in the bloodstream, this can result in fatigue, slowed processing speed, and inertia.

According to 3,500 ADDitude survey responses, 57 to 78 percent of stimulant medication users experience a regular crash, with dextroamphetamine and Ritalin LA users reporting the highest prevalence. Even people taking the most popular stimulant medications reported crash prevalence rates of near or above 60 percent. (Users’ experiences with the most popular stimulant medications are shown in the chart below.) The lowest crash prevalence rates were reported by people taking the non-stimulant medications Atomoxetine/Strattera (40%) and guanfacine (52.9%), suggesting that medication crashes are less common with non-stimulant ADHD treatments.

Readers did not cite medication interactions or caffeine as significant contributors.

The ability to manage household responsibilities is “often” or “always” impaired by medication crashes for 70 percent of survey respondents. Half of crashers say work responsibilities “often” or “always” suffer, and 43 percent say social and family interactions suffer.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The building will feature a central venue that has massive bamboo support elements based on local drums.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ecuadorian studio Caá Porá Arquitectura has teamed up with US-based Jerome Haferd Studio and engineer Juan Sebastián Pérez for the Bombódromo performance centre in Carchi, Ecuador.

The building will feature a central venue that has massive bamboo support elements based on local drums.

The campus will include dozens of buildings centred around a massive auditorium in the province of Carchi, north of Quito, sited along the Chota River in an Andean valley.

Masterplanned by Caá Porá Arquitectura, the campus was designed for local government to celebrate Afro-Ecuadorian culture.

Based on this, the central performance centre has a design based on the bomba, a drum used by local people.

“The inspiration for a lot of the design language was kind of to bridge African and Andean kind of design languages and ancestral aesthetics,” Jerome Haferd told Dezeen.

“That is embodied in the bomba drum, which is a unique instrument that is made by the people in this region, who we worked with very closely to come up with the design concept for the master plan.”.

“[The bomba] was adapted and generated out of materials local to this valley in Ecuador, and so it’s really a hybrid between the Andean mountains and Africa.”.

The main performance space, designed to hold more than 10,000, will have massive bundles of laminated bamboo supporting a roof system 30 metres in diameter.

These bundled columns have been designed to feature laminated bamboo and timber elements, reflecting the construction of the bomba drum and local construction methods more generally.

Acoustic fabric will hang from the wooden rafters of the semi-enclosed performance space.

A series of stone buildings will flank the main performance space, forming the back-of-house facilities.

An outdoor area will feature a tiered gathering space tucked into the low-lying trees around the river and provide the main viewing platforms for the performances.

As many as eight outbuildings will feature on the campus, including classrooms, a restaurant and artisan kiosks.

These structures will be built with metal roofs and rammed-earth walls, furthering the connection to local building techniques.

“The result is a radical, place-based reinterpretation of how a performing arts venue can respond to a unique cultural context while accommodating flexible uses,” noted the team, which worked with local group Fundación Casa Oshun for the community outreach.

The project is expected to break ground in 2027.

Recently, a team including SANAA, Caá Porá Arquitectura, Estudio A0 and Jerome Haferd Studio was selected to design the National Museum of Ecuador in Quito, after the original design was cancelled following community backlash.

The Urgency of Early ADHD Intervention

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (870 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, delaying treatment for ADHD until the teen years comes with potential life-long consequences.
  • Q: I believe my elementary school-age child has ADHD, but my husband doesn’t think so.
  • This question reflects a dilemma faced by many families: What happens when one parent wants possible signs of ADHD evaluated while another prefers to wait and see?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, delaying treatment for ADHD until the teen years comes with potential life-long consequences. Here’s what you should know.

Q: I believe my elementary school-age child has ADHD, but my husband doesn’t think so. He refuses to get our child evaluated. I have ADHD and I know this can run in families. What should I do?

This question reflects a dilemma faced by many families: What happens when one parent wants possible signs of ADHD evaluated while another prefers to wait and see? The answer may matter more than many people realize.

Imagine two children entering first grade:.

Jacob is bright, curious, and energetic. He struggles to sit still, frequently forgets to turn in his homework, and has difficulty following multi-step instructions. His teacher notices the symptoms and relays these to his parents. Jacob’s pediatrician conducts a comprehensive evaluation and diagnoses Jacob with ADHD.

His parents learn strategies to support him at home. His school implements accommodations. Later, medication becomes part of his treatment plan. Jacob still faces challenges, but he learns how his brain works and develops tools to succeed. He graduates from high school with strong grades and heads off to college.

[Webinar Replay: “6 Principles for Raising a Child with ADHD”].

Now imagine Maya. She is also intelligent, but her suspected ADHD symptoms present differently. She daydreams in class and quietly falls behind. She is emotionally sensitive, often taking criticism to heart and becoming overwhelmed by setbacks that her peers seem to brush off. Her teachers describe her as capable but inconsistent. Because she isn’t disruptive, her struggles are attributed to a lack of effort, disorganization, anxiety, or immaturity.

According to recent reports, year after year, she works harder while feeling increasingly frustrated. As academic demands increase, so do her feelings of self-doubt and inadequacy. By the time she receives an ADHD diagnosis at age 16, her grades have suffered, her confidence has eroded, and she is considering leaving school altogether.

The paths of these two children, one who received early intervention with medication and one who remained untreated until her mid-teens, illustrate a growing concern in ADHD care: It’s not simply about whether children are diagnosed, but when.

[Self-Test: Could Your Preschooler Have ADHD?].

A recent study published in JAMA Psychiatry examined educational outcomes among more than 580,000 individuals with ADHD. The researchers found that children diagnosed earlier in life had significantly better educational outcomes than those diagnosed during adolescence. Earlier diagnosis with associated with higher grade point averages, a greater likelihood of pursuing academic educational tracks, and substantially lower rates of school dropout.

Recent findings suggest that the differences were striking. Individuals diagnosed during the early elementary school years had school dropout rates of approximately 9 percent by age 20, compared with nearly 30 percent among those first diagnosed around age 16. Similar patterns were observed in both males and females. The researchers concluded that adolescents diagnosed later represent a particularly vulnerable group.

It has been revealed that the findings do not suggest that a diagnosis alone changes a child’s future. Rather, earlier recognition creates opportunities for intervention. Children identified sooner can access school accommodations, behavioral supports, parent education, and, when appropriate, medication – before years of academic struggles, self-doubt, and declining confidence take hold and begin to shape their identity.

This raises an notable question: How many Mayas are sitting in classrooms today, struggling silently while waiting years for recognition or a diagnosis?

Universal ADHD screening offers a potential solution. Many children with ADHD are identified only after academic, social, or emotional difficulties have become impossible to ignore. Screening creates an opportunity to recognize concerns earlier before the consequences of undiagnosed ADHD begin to accumulate. Importantly, screening is not diagnosis. It is simply an invitation to look more closely.

Industry observers note that many critics of universal screening worry about overdiagnosis or unnecessary labeling. Those concerns deserve consideration. However, screening itself does not determine whether a child has ADHD. It merely identifies children who may benefit from a more comprehensive evaluation, meaning that fewer children with significant challenges get overlooked.

Recent findings suggest that growing evidence suggests that every year of delayed recognition carries educational and emotional costs that are difficult to reverse. Universal screening will not identify every child. But it may help more children find the right path before they wander too far afield.

Recent findings suggest that for many children, the greatest risk may not be receiving an ADHD diagnosis. It may be never receiving one at all.

25 types of meditation and how to choose the right one

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3216 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • Recent findings suggest that the benefits of meditation can reach across your well-being, from reducing stress and anxiety to improving focus and supporting mental and emotional health.
  • Recent findings suggest that we’ve grouped the many types of meditation into six families, so you can see how they relate before you pick one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA.

Recent findings suggest that the benefits of meditation can reach across your well-being, from reducing stress and anxiety to improving focus and supporting mental and emotional health. But there’s a catch: meditation is a wide family of practices, and the type that works beautifully for your friend might leave you fidgety and frustrated.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve grouped the many types of meditation into six families, so you can see how they relate before you pick one. Think of it as a menu. Try whichever one draws you in, and let your practice change as you do.

Meditation is a way to train our attention and awareness so we can be more present in the moment. Most types ask you to rest your focus somewhere, like the breath, a word, a sensation, or a movement, and to notice without judgment when your mind drifts, then return. That returning, over and over, is the practice.

What changes from one type to the next is where you place your attention and what you hope to cultivate. Some practices sharpen focus, while others cultivate compassion or help the body relax. Many share a thread of mindfulness, noticing where your attention drifts and gently coming back.

With a history rooted in the spiritual traditions of the East, including Buddhism, Hinduism, and Taoism, meditation has long been recognized as a means to gain enlightenment, self-realization, and balance.

By exploring the different forms of meditation practice, you can discover what works best for you to enhance your overall well-being.

These practices share a common aim. You anchor your attention in the present moment and meet whatever arises without judgment. They're a good place to start if you're fresh to meditation.

Industry observers note that particularly accessible to beginners, mindfulness meditation invites you to immerse yourself in the present moment. It teaches you to observe your thoughts, feelings, and physical sensations without judgment. By focusing on the breath or the sensations in the body, rather than worries about the past or future, you learn to anchor yourself in the now. This can lead to reduced stress and improved well-being.

Read more: How to practice mindfulness meditation: 8 tips to get started.

Sources indicate that A body scan moves your attention slowly through the body, one area at a time, noticing sensation without trying to change it. It's a core mindfulness technique and a gentle way into the practice, since you always have your body to come back to. Many people use it to unwind before sleep.

Read more: Body scan meditation: a step-by-step guide to practice.

Here the breath is your anchor. You rest your attention on each inhale and exhale, without trying to control the rhythm, and return to it whenever your mind wanders. Because your breath is always with you, this is one of the most portable practices you can carry into a stressful moment.

Read more: How to practice breath meditation to relieve stress.

Mindful eating brings full attention to a meal through the senses: the color, smell, texture, and taste of your food, and the signals of hunger and fullness. It can support digestion and help you notice emotional eating patterns with more kindness.

Read more: How mindful eating can boost your mental and physical health.

Recent findings suggest that focus is the whole point here. You rest your attention on one thing, a flame, a sound, or a word, and return to it each time the mind strays. Over time this can sharpen your attention and prepare you for deeper states.

It has been revealed that concentration meditation is a practice of focused attention, where the mind is directed toward a single point of reference, such as a candle flame, a sound, or the breath. This can help develop focus and attentiveness in everyday life and prepare the mind for deeper states of meditation. This practice can be especially helpful for students, professionals, or anyone looking to improve their cognitive abilities and productivity.

Read more: Concentration meditation: what is it and how to practice?

Mantra meditation involves the silent repetition of a word or phrase, known as a mantra, to focus the mind and bring deeper states of meditation. This practice can be found in many spiritual traditions worldwide and serves as a powerful tool for calming the mind, reducing stress, and enhancing spiritual growth and a sense of peace and clarity. If you find yourself easily distracted or struggling with a busy mind, mantra meditation can help you maintain focus.

Read more: Mantra meditation: what it is, benefits, and how to practice.

Om meditation is a form of mantra practice built around chanting or silently repeating the sound "Om." The vibration of the sound gives the mind something to settle on, and many practitioners find the repetition grounding.

In a recent development, read more: What is Om meditation? Plus, a step-by-step guide to practice.

Also called trataka, candle meditation uses the soft glow of a flame as your focal point. You rest your gaze on the candle, placed at eye level a short distance away, and let it hold your attention. It's a visual anchor for anyone who finds eyes-closed practice restless.

Read more: Candle meditation: a step-by-step guide to practice at home.

Visualization meditation guides you to picture a scene, place, or outcome in vivid detail, such as somewhere you feel calm and safe. By giving the mind a rich image to rest on, it can lower stress and support a sense of ease. Unlike open mindfulness, it actively directs the imagination.

Read more: Visualization meditation: 8 exercises to add to your practice.

Recent findings suggest that warmth is the thread running through this family, directed toward yourself, the people you love, and even those you struggle with. These practices can enhance empathy and strengthen your relationships.

Compassion meditation aims to cultivate feelings of love, kindness, and compassion toward yourself and others. It involves silently directing sentiments of goodwill toward loved ones, acquaintances, and even people we might have a difficult relationship with. It encourages us to see beyond our differences, nurturing a sense of connectedness. A traditional example is Tonglen, a Tibetan practice that pairs the breath with compassion for suffering.

Read more: Compassion meditation: what it is, benefits, & how to practice.

11. Loving-kindness meditation (metta).

Loving-kindness, or Metta meditation, is a practice of cultivating an attitude of unconditional love and kindness towards all beings. It starts with developing a loving acceptance of yourself and gradually extends outward to include friends, family, strangers, and even those with whom we may have conflicts. This practice can help break down barriers of anger and division, promoting peace and connection. Though loving-kindness meditation and compassion meditation are closely related and often practiced together, loving-kindness meditation involves sending wishes of happiness, well-being, and peace to yourself and others, whereas compassion meditation specifically focuses on suffering, understanding it, feeling it, and wishing for it to be alleviated.

Read more: Loving-kindness meditation: what it is, how to practice and why.

According to recent reports, gratitude meditation guides your attention toward what you appreciate, often by calling to mind a few people or moments you're thankful for. Practiced in the morning or evening, it can lower anxiety and support better sleep, and it pairs naturally with compassion practice.

Read more: How gratitude meditation can help reduce anxiety.

Recent findings suggest that sitting still doesn't suit everyone. If stillness makes you restless, these practices let you meditate while the body is in motion, with your attention on each movement.

Sources indicate that moving meditation brings together deliberate movement and a focused mind. You move with purpose, noticing each step, stretch, or breath as you go. Yoga, tai chi, mindful stretching, and mindful dancing all fall under this heading, and it can be done almost anywhere.

Read more: The benefits of moving meditation and how to start practicing.

Walking meditation means walking slowly and deliberately, with your attention fully on the act of walking: each step, the movement of your legs, the ground beneath your feet, and your breath. It turns an everyday activity into a practice you can take outdoors.

Read more: Walking meditation: how to practice and its benefits.

Mindful movement is the broad practice of bringing present-moment awareness to how your body moves, whether through stretching, yoga, or simple everyday motion. It's mindfulness carried into the body rather than held in stillness.

Read more: What is mindful movement? Plus 9 ways to get started.

Qigong is a traditional Chinese practice that combines movement, breathwork, and meditation to support balance and focus. In its active form you meditate while flowing through slow, deliberate movements, which makes it a bridge between exercise and stillness.

Read more: What is qigong? Benefits, types, and how to practice.

Sources indicate that yoga nidra, sometimes called yogic sleep, is a guided rest practice done lying down. A teacher or recording leads you through stages of body scan, breath, and visualization into a state between waking and sleep. No yoga experience is needed, and it's often used for deep rest at bedtime.

Read more: What is yoga nidra? Plus, why it may be your new BFF at bedtime.

A few practices are rooted in a specific lineage and tend to go deeper, often taught within a tradition or by a teacher. Several come from Buddhism, while others, like Transcendental Meditation and kundalini, come from Hindu and Vedic traditions.

Buddhist meditation is the broad tradition behind many of the best-known techniques, including Zen and Vipassana below, along with loving-kindness. If you want a feel for the tradition as a whole before exploring the specific practices, start here.

Read more: Buddhist meditation: types, techniques & how to practice.

Zen meditation, or Zazen, is a disciplined form of meditation central to Zen Buddhism. You sit in a specific posture, focusing on the breath while observing thoughts and sensations as they arise and pass without attachment. Zazen emphasizes the importance of moment-to-moment awareness for a profound sense of peace and insight.

Read more: Zen meditation: how (and why) to start a Zen practice.

Vipassana, which means "to see things as they really are," is one of India's most ancient techniques of meditation. It focuses on the deep interconnection between mind and body. Through disciplined attention to physical sensations, you can develop insight into the nature of impermanence, suffering, and egolessness, to move toward enlightenment and liberation. Vipassana meditation is challenging, yet rewarding, offering profound insights into our own minds.

Read more: Vipassana meditation: what it is, benefits & how to practice.

Sources indicate that 21. Transcendental Meditation (TM).

Transcendental Meditation comes from the Hindu and Vedic tradition and was brought to the West in the mid-20th century. It's a silent, mantra-based practice, typically done for about 20 minutes twice a day, and it's taught one-on-one by a certified teacher who gives you your mantra. It's described as effortless, letting the mantra gently carry the mind toward deep rest.

Read more: Transcendental Meditation versus mindfulness meditation.

Kundalini meditation is a spiritual practice that aims to awaken what the tradition describes as an inner energy at the base of the spine, using breathwork, posture, and chanting. Practitioners describe effects in spiritual and energetic terms, which are rooted in belief rather than established science. Because the breathwork can be intense, check with your doctor first if you have respiratory, heart, or blood pressure concerns.

Recent findings suggest that read more: What is Kundalini meditation? Plus, how to try it yourself.

In a recent development, chakra meditation focuses attention on the body's energy centers, or chakras, often by visualizing each as a spinning wheel, chanting a sound for each one, or breathing into each area. As with kundalini, the idea of chakras comes from spiritual tradition and is described as belief rather than scientific fact.

Read more: Chakra meditation: what it is, benefits & how to practice.

Recent findings suggest that this family works from the body inward. The practices help your nervous system slow down and your muscles release tension, which makes them a good entry point when stress reveals up physically.

Relaxation meditation is an umbrella term for any practice that helps the body release tension and the mind wind down. It often draws on breathing, body awareness, or guided sessions, and it's a gentle place to begin if deeper practices feel like a lot right now.

A sound bath, where you lie back and listen to instruments, is one example.

Read more: 5 relaxation meditations that actually work.

Sources indicate that 25. Progressive muscle relaxation.

It has been revealed that progressive muscle relaxation guides you to tense and then release each muscle group in turn, usually working from the feet up to the face. By targeting the physical side of stress, it can ease tension that anxiety stores in the body, and it pairs well with a body scan to finish.

Read more: What is progressive muscle relaxation (and how to practice it).

Recent findings suggest that the six families above group the 25 types by where your attention goes. This table puts them side by side, so you can compare meditation types and see where to start.

There’s no one-size-fits-all approach to meditation, and your needs may change over time. The best meditation technique is the one that feels right for you now and fits into your life. These five steps can help you find it.

Reflect on your goals: Think about what you're hoping to achieve. Whether it's reducing stress, finding inner peace, or developing compassion, your goals can guide your choice of practice.

Experiment with different practices: Try out different meditation methods and resources, including the Calm app, online courses, and local meditation groups, for guided sessions in different styles.

Listen to your body and mind: Pay attention to how you feel during and after meditation. The right practice should leave you feeling calm and refreshed. If you feel frustrated or strained, try a different type.

It has been revealed that be patient and open-minded: Finding the meditation practice that works for you can take time. Approach each type with curiosity, allowing your experiences to guide your journey.

Seek guidance: If you're unsure where to start, seek advice from experienced practitioners or meditation teachers for support tailored to your personal journey.

Starting a meditation practice can bring greater mindfulness and improved emotional well-being. However, establishing a consistent practice can feel daunting. By bringing these tips into your approach, you can build a meditation practice that fits your life and becomes a source of strength and peace.

Industry observers note that A consistent routine is vital in establishing any new habit, including meditation. Identify a time of day when you can dedicate a few uninterrupted minutes to your practice. For many, morning meditation sets a positive tone for the day ahead. However, if evenings or another time fits your schedule better, make that your meditation moment. Find a quiet, comfortable spot where you can sit or lie down without distractions.

💙 Morning person? Try this Morning Meditation to set your tone for the rest of the day. Nighttime person? This Deep Rest meditation is for you.

Sources indicate that begin with just a few minutes each day. Even a short period of meditation can have significant benefits, and starting small makes the practice feel more manageable. As you become more comfortable with the process, you can gradually extend your meditation time.

💙 Begin your meditation journey with Jeff Warren in this Meditation for Beginners series.

Meditation is a personal experience, and there’s no single "right" way to do it. Many people form expectations based on others' descriptions, but each person's meditation journey is unique. You don’t need to empty your mind or feel bliss in every session. Notice your thoughts and feelings without judgment, and meet whatever comes up with kindness and curiosity.

💙 Explore how having Expectations can affect us and our lives with Tamara Levitt on the Daily Calm.

It has been revealed that physical discomfort can be a distraction during meditation. To help settle your body and prepare for stillness, consider some gentle stretching or mindful movement, such as yoga or tai chi, before you begin. This can help release tension in the body and allow you to sit more comfortably.

💙 Follow along with The Daily Move’s Releasing Stress session to help you unwind before settling down.

Guided meditations, available through apps, websites, or local classes, can provide verbal instructions and cues to lead you through the meditation process. They can introduce you to different types of meditation, help keep your focus, and offer insights into how to handle common challenges like wandering thoughts or restlessness.

💙 Try this guided meditation to help you with Reframing Difficult Thoughts whenever your thoughts start to overwhelm you.

It’s normal to encounter challenges as you begin your meditation practice. You might miss a day or find your mind wandering constantly. When this happens, treat yourself with kindness and compassion. Each time you notice your mind has drifted and come back to the present moment, you’re practicing.

💙 Practice this Loving Kindness meditation to guide you in cultivating feelings of kindness toward yourself and others.

Industry observers note that join a meditation group or find a community of practitioners that can provide support and a sense of connection. Sharing experiences with others on a similar path can be incredibly encouraging.

There’s no single agreed list, but these three approaches are often used to sort the many types of meditation:.

Concentration meditation: You rest your attention on a single point of reference, such as the breath, a mantra, a sound, or a candle flame. When your mind wanders, you return to it.

Mindfulness meditation: You widen your awareness to include thoughts, sensations, and your surroundings as they arise. It is often taught as part of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR).

Loving-kindness meditation (Metta): You build goodwill and warmth toward others, starting with yourself.

The idea of levels in meditation can vary depending on the tradition or practice. A way to think of meditation depth might include the different types and states.

Physical relaxation: The initial stage where the body relaxes deeply.

Concentration: The mind begins to focus, reducing distractions.

Mindful awareness: A state of heightened awareness of the present moment.

Deepening peace: Inner silence becomes more profound.

Insight: Understanding about yourself and reality may arise.

Blissful states: Experiences of joy or profound contentment.

Transcendence: A sense of unity or oneness with all, often considered the deepest level of meditation.

Industry observers note that the power of a meditation practice can vary from person to person, depending on individual needs, preferences, and goals. Some may find mindfulness meditation helpful for managing stress and enhancing self-awareness, while others prefer the structured approach of Transcendental Meditation or the heart-opening practices of loving-kindness meditation.

Ultimately, the most ‘powerful’ type is the one you’ll keep practicing. Try a few to see which fits.

Industry News: Easy Eggplant Bolognese (1 Pot!)

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that bolognese is an Italian sauce that gets its name from the Italian city of Bologna.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When we add another bolognese to the blog (Yes, we already have versions 1, 2, 3, and 4), you know it’s something special! This newest version is made with EGGPLANT, meaning it’s the perfect bolognese for late summer. It’s light yet satisfying, creamy yet bright, and full of bold Italian-inspired flavor — everyone will be asking for seconds!

Even better? It’s a breeze to make — just 1 pot required! What are you waiting for? Get that pasta water boiling!

It has been revealed that bolognese is an Italian sauce that gets its name from the Italian city of Bologna. It’s typically made with meat, soffrito (onions, celery, and carrots), white wine, milk, and tomato paste or sauce, all simmered to create a rich, flavorful sauce.

Recent findings suggest that our eggplant version strays from the traditional as it excludes meat (and includes eggplant) and incorporates dairy alternatives. But the rest of the dish is very similar to traditional bolognese and feels so hearty it might convert even the most adamant veggie skeptics!

It has been revealed that this 1-pot eggplant bolognese is everything you want for a cozy pasta night, minus the fuss! It starts with sautéing onion and carrots to create a simple, savory-sweet base. Next, we add eggplant (cut into very small cubes) and let it sauté until it has softened and browned (hello, flavor!).

According to recent reports, build the flavor even further with garlic and red pepper flakes and by deglazing the pan with wine. Crushed tomatoes and tomato paste ensure a bright, tomato-forward sauce, and a small amount of dairy-free milk (we like homemade cashew milk) gives it a gentle creaminess and richness. #10381. What is EMDR therapy, and does it actually work?

What is EMDR therapy, and does it actually work?

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1671 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Maybe a friend swears EMDR helped her move past something she’d carried for years.
  • If you’re uncertain, that’s understandable, because EMDR can sound unconventional: you briefly recall a painful memory while following side-to-side stimulation, like tracking a moving target with your eyes.
  • Here’s what EMDR involves, what the research reveals, and what a session is like, so you have a clearer picture of whether it might make sense for you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

Maybe a friend swears EMDR helped her move past something she’d carried for years. Or maybe you came across it online while searching for ways to cope with a memory that still feels heavy. Whether you’ve heard of EMDR but don’t know how it works, or you’re familiar with the approach but skeptical, we’re here to break it all down.

If you’re uncertain, that’s understandable, because EMDR can sound unconventional: you briefly recall a painful memory while following side-to-side stimulation, like tracking a moving target with your eyes. But the research tells a more reassuring story. It’s a well-studied therapy for trauma, and it’s increasingly explored for anxiety and depression, too.

Here’s what EMDR involves, what the research reveals, and what a session is like, so you have a clearer picture of whether it might make sense for you.

EMDR stands for eye movement desensitization and reprocessing. It’s a structured therapy that helps the brain reprocess distressing memories so they carry less emotional weight. Psychologist Francine Shapiro, PhD, developed it in the late 1980s after she noticed that certain eye movements seemed to ease her own troubling thoughts.

According to recent reports, EMDR rests on Shapiro’s adaptive information processing model. The idea is that your brain normally files an experience away, so you can recall it later without feeling like you’re living it again. But a frightening or painful event can interrupt that process, leaving the memory raw and unfiled, still carrying the fear and detail of that moment. That’s why it can resurface later, as vivid as the day it happened.

Industry observers note that according to this model, “processing” a memory means helping your brain finish the filing. You don’t forget what happened, and the facts don’t change. What changes is the emotional charge it carries, so recalling it feels less like reliving it and more like remembering it. To help that happen, EMDR uses a technique called “bilateral stimulation.”.

Industry observers note that EMDR uses a technique called bilateral stimulation. While you hold a difficult memory in mind, a trained therapist guides you through side-to-side stimulation.

Bilateral stimulation can take a few forms:.

eye movements that follow your therapist’s fingers.

gentle taps that switch between your hands or knees.

tones that play in one ear, then the other.

There’s a theory behind the side-to-side part, though researchers are still working out exactly why it helps. The leading explanation is about mental bandwidth. Your working memory, the part of your mind that holds what you’re focused on right now, can only handle so much at once. When you track side-to-side movement while recalling a hard memory, the two tasks compete for that limited space. The hard memory tends to feel a little less vivid, and with repetition it can lose its sharp edges, so it feels less overwhelming to hold.

💙 Learn more in our guide to bilateral stimulation.

EMDR has eight phases, though they tend to blend together in practice. The early phases cover your history and teach you coping skills, so you feel prepared before any hard memories arise. In the middle phases, you focus on a specific memory while following bilateral stimulation, which is meant to help your brain reprocess it. The final phases check that the memory feels less distressing and help you close out the work safely.

The evidence is strong for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), a condition that can develop after a frightening or life-threatening event. A Cochrane review (a gold-standard summary of research on a topic) found that EMDR and trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) both reduce PTSD symptoms. They also outperformed other therapies when researchers checked in after treatment ended. A 2024 review in the Journal of Traumatic Stress identified more than 30 randomized controlled trials supporting EMDR for PTSD in adults and children. Major health organizations, including the World Health Organization, recommend EMDR for PTSD.

However, some guidelines, including those from the American Psychological Association (APA), rate the evidence for EMDR as less certain than for trauma-focused CBT. Researchers also debate exactly why EMDR works.

💙 Read more about how EMDR can help you cope with PTSD.

The picture is more mixed outside PTSD. Early research suggests EMDR may help with anxiety, as one meta-analysis found reduced symptoms of anxiety, panic, and phobia, though the studies were small and varied in quality.

Evidence for depression is emerging as well. Another meta-analysis demonstrated reduced depression symptoms, with the strongest effects in more severe cases. These findings are promising, but they don’t carry the same weight as the PTSD research.

In a recent development, after you and a therapist finish the early phases, you bring a specific memory to mind and notice the thoughts and body sensations that come with it. Then your therapist guides you through the bilateral stimulation while you let your mind go where it goes. You can ask to pause or stop at any time. Unlike many talk therapies, EMDR doesn’t require you to describe the memory in detail.

It has been revealed that sessions usually run 60–90 minutes. Your therapist pauses often to check in on what you noticed. Over several rounds of bilateral stimulation, many people find the memory feels less sharp, even though the facts don’t change. Between sessions, a mindfulness practice, such as slow breathing or a body scan, can help you ease feelings that surface.

💙 Explore Calm's EMDR-Inspired Bilateral: Anxiety, a set of music tracks that alternate gently between your left and right ear. It draws on the bilateral stimulation used in EMDR, though audio-only versions haven’t been studied on their own the way clinical EMDR has. Think of it as a calming complement to therapy, not a replacement for a trained therapist.

The answer varies, since it depends on what you’re working through. For a single, recent trauma, some people notice their symptoms ease within a handful of sessions. More complex or long-standing trauma usually takes longer, sometimes many months. Therapists describe a typical course as 6–12 sessions, though it varies widely from person to person.

It has been revealed that along the way, some people feel worse before they feel better. Painful memories can stir up strong emotions in the short term, which is common and doesn’t mean EMDR isn’t working. Before reprocessing begins, your therapist teaches you coping skills, such as grounding exercises that anchor you in the present, so you have tools to use if those feelings get intense.

💙 Try the 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 practice, a quick way to ground yourself in the present, with Prof. Megan Reitz.

Recent findings suggest that EMDR stands for eye movement desensitization and reprocessing. It’s a form of therapy that uses bilateral stimulation, such as guided eye movements, to help your brain process distressing memories so they feel less intense. Psychologist Francine Shapiro developed this therapy in the late 1980s.

In a recent development, EMDR may help with anxiety, though PTSD is where the evidence is strongest. The studies on anxiety are smaller and less consistent. If your anxiety is tied to a specific frightening experience, it may be worth asking a therapist whether EMDR fits your situation.

💙 Explore how mindfulness can help you manage your anxiety.

EMDR differs from talk therapy because it doesn’t require you to describe your experience in detail. You’ll still talk with your therapist, especially early on, but the reprocessing happens while you hold a memory in mind and follow bilateral stimulation. Talk therapies like cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) focus more on examining and reshaping your thoughts out loud.

The main benefit of EMDR is that it can ease the distress tied to painful memories. For many people with PTSD, that can mean fewer flashbacks and less of that constant, on-alert feeling.

Much of the debate is about why EMDR works, not whether it does. The evidence is strongest for PTSD, with early and more mixed findings for anxiety and depression.

Some studies suggest the eye movements themselves add little. The benefit may instead come from giving your mind a second task while you recall a memory, which can make it feel less vivid and emotionally intense. Other tasks that split your attention may have the same effect.

According to recent reports, certain guidelines, including the APA’s, consider the evidence for EMDR less established than for trauma-focused CBT. None of this takes away from the relief many people find with EMDR. It’s useful context as you weigh your options with a therapist.

EMDR is generally safe when a trained therapist delivers it, though you may experience some short-term effects. You might feel more emotional or tired between sessions, or have vivid dreams as your brain keeps processing the memory.

Industry observers note that these reactions usually pass within a day or two. If they last longer or feel overwhelming, it’s a good idea to tell your therapist, who can adjust the pace with you. Serious side effects are uncommon when a therapist follows the full eight-phase process.

It has been revealed that the number of sessions you need depends on the memory you’re addressing and how long it has affected you. Some people feel relief after a few sessions, while longer-standing experiences often take more time. A common range is 6–12 sessions, but your timeline may be shorter or longer. Your therapist can give you a better sense of what to expect once they know your history.

Full EMDR needs a trained therapist, so it’s not something to try on your own. A therapist helps you reprocess memories and stay grounded if one feels overwhelming, which matters most with intense trauma.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition?
  • Could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition?
  • Fluoride in community drinking water is not linked to lower adolescent IQ or poorer thinking skills later in life, a long-running US study finds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

Could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

Fluoride in community drinking water is not linked to lower adolescent IQ or poorer thinking skills later in life, a long-running US study finds.

Researchers followed a generation of Wisconsin school-leavers, examining cognitive performance from adolescence into their eighties.

Those exposed to fluoridated water did not show a consistent disadvantage compared with people whose communities had no fluoridation.

The findings address concerns that adding fluoride to drinking water to prevent tooth decay could undermine intellectual development.

Professor John Robert Warren, the study’s first author, said:.

“Utah, Florida and many municipalities have chosen to remove fluoride from drinking water based on flawed studies that considered the IQ effects of exposure to massive doses of fluoride.

Sources indicate that because levels of fluoride added to municipal drinking water in the U.S. are so much lower, almost all prior evidence from those international studies is not relevant to U.S. public policy debates.”.

The research draws on the Wisconsin Longitudinal Study, which began with over 10,000 people who graduated from high school in 1957.

Researchers combined school IQ records with historical information about community water fluoridation and naturally occurring fluoride levels.

Following participants into old age allowed researchers to examine whether childhood exposure was associated with lasting differences in cognitive performance.

Comparing communities requires care because their residents can differ in ways that also relate to cognitive performance.

Once those background differences were taken into account, there was no consistent evidence that exposure was associated with either better or worse performance.

The same broad pattern appeared when researchers focused on people who had lived in the same county since early childhood, increasing confidence in their estimates of exposure.

Overall, the findings suggest that growing up with fluoridated community water is not associated with poorer cognitive performance in old age.

The study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (Warren et al., 2026).

#10376. Can you be friends with your ex? What to consider first

Can you be friends with your ex? What to consider first

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1443 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s your ex, sending a meme you would’ve laughed at together six months ago.
  • Moments like this are why staying friends with an ex can feel so confusing.
  • Whether you’re the one hoping to stay in touch or the one being asked to, here’s how to tell if staying friends would help you move on or make it harder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your phone buzzes. It’s your ex, sending a meme you would’ve laughed at together six months ago. You smile, then wonder why you smiled.

Moments like this are why staying friends with an ex can feel so confusing. For some people, staying connected feels natural because the habit, and maybe the care, is still there. For others, it makes healing feel harder. Every situation is different, and you’re allowed to take your time figuring out what works for you.

Whether you’re the one hoping to stay in touch or the one being asked to, here’s how to tell if staying friends would help you move on or make it harder.

In some cases, you may be able to. Post-breakup friendships can be healthy and meaningful when the breakup was mutual, the relationship had little conflict, and both people have had time to grieve.

According to recent reports, that said, every friendship between exes is different. Researchers who study friendships after breakups describe two kinds. In one, both people have moved on and value the connection. In the other, one or both people stay in touch because of lingering attraction or reluctance to end things. The first kind can be rewarding. The second can make it harder to get over the breakup.

The dynamic you had with your ex matters, too. A study found that relationships shaped by high conflict, emotional dependency, or attachment anxiety may be harder to turn into a friendship afterward.

In a recent development, before you decide anything, it may help to reflect on why you want to stay in touch. A few questions to sit with:.

What am I hoping this friendship gives me?

Am I trying to stay close to them or avoid the discomfort of letting go?

How would I feel if they started dating someone new?

If the last question stings, it may just mean that you need more time.

It has been revealed that if you were the one who ended things, you might want friendship out of guilt or a wish to soften the loss. If you were the one who was left, you might view friendship as a potential path to getting back together.

If the answers don’t come right away, try a mindfulness practice. A few minutes of reflection or a short breathing exercise can help you sort through what you’re thinking and feeling.

💙 Try the Pause to Check In meditation on the Calm app.

According to recent reports, if you’ve thought it through and still want to stay in touch, a few signs suggest a friendship may work. People who are securely attached often find it easier to stay friends after a breakup, but the list below can apply to anyone:.

You both see the breakup as mutual, with no ongoing hurt, resentment, or blame.

You’ve both accepted that the romantic relationship is over, with no unresolved romantic feelings.

There’s a reason for the friendship beyond comfort or familiarity, such as shared values, kids together, or a work connection.

In certain cases, staying friends can make healing harder or keep you from pouring energy into newly introduced parts of your life:.

You’re still in love with your ex and hoping the friendship leads somewhere.

The relationship involved emotional manipulation, control, or abuse.

The friendship gets in the way of upcoming relationships, like when a new partner feels uneasy about your connection.

You have different expectations for the friendship, which could leave one of you hurt.

💙 Discover the signs of having a toxic ex.

According to recent reports, it can be, especially since staying in touch can make it harder to let go. One study found that regular contact with an ex may slow emotional recovery. When you’re still part of each other’s routines, it can be harder to mourn the end of the relationship.

By contrast, a low-contact friendship, where you talk occasionally and keep to limits you’ve agreed on, is less likely to hold either of you back.

How you feel after you talk is worth paying attention to. If you often feel sad, anxious, or unsettled, or you keep replaying the conversation, it may help to take some space.

💙 Read more on how to deal with a breakup when you’re hurting.

Industry observers note that it may be appropriate to be friends with your ex, depending on your situation. It tends to work best when you’ve both moved on, the breakup didn’t involve harm, and the friendship fits both of your lives. If it also feels honest and comfortable to you, that’s a good sign.

According to recent reports, being friends with an ex isn’t automatically a red flag. If your partner is friends with an ex, how they handle it matters more than the friendship itself. A few questions to consider:.

Transparency: Do they talk about it openly, or does it feel secretive?

Priorities: Do they make time for you and the relationship?

Boundaries: Are there clear limits on the friendship, or does contact feel constant and undefined?

Responsiveness: When you raise a concern, does your partner listen or dismiss it?

If something doesn’t sit right, you could bring it up and see whether they listen, get defensive, or brush you off. If you’re the one staying friends with an ex, your new partner’s concerns are worth hearing out, even if nothing is wrong.

Industry observers note that you don’t have to keep in touch with your ex after a breakup. Taking space is often healthy and necessary, and you can change your mind later. You can choose a full break, a time-limited break (“let’s not talk for a few months”), or a low-contact friendship.

If you do stay in touch, some boundaries may protect your well-being. A few to consider:.

It has been revealed that set a pace. Daily texting can pull you back into old routines, so try starting with occasional check-ins instead.

Decide what’s off limits. That might mean dating lives, old conflicts, and late-night “remember when” talks.

Give yourself space online. Mute or unfollow for a while to adjust without ending the connection.

Sources indicate that blueprint a review and a way out. After a few months, ask whether the friendship still feels good. If it doesn’t, have a line ready, like “I think I need to take a step back for now.”.

Recent findings suggest that if you share children, a workplace, or a friend group, you may need to stay in touch. It’s often best to stick to logistics, like pickup times for the kids or project deadlines at work.

💙 Explore the Boundaries meditation on Calm.

Sources indicate that there’s no set amount of time to wait before trying to be friends with an ex. Some people feel ready within months, while others take years. Some never feel ready or choose not to be friends, and that’s okay.

According to recent reports, A question to ask yourself is whether you can feel okay about the thought of your ex moving on. If that still hurts, you probably need more time.

Yes, being friends with an ex can sometimes turn into getting back together. Whether that’s a good thing depends on why your relationship ended and whether those reasons have changed.

Sources indicate that problems tied to circumstances, like bad timing or distance, may be easier to work through than core differences, like values, long-term goals, or how you communicate. If you get back together and those core differences haven’t changed, the same patterns can resurface.

It’s painful when one of you wants to stay friends after a breakup and the other doesn’t, and what helps depends on which side you’re on.

In a recent development, if you’re the one being asked, you’re allowed to say “not yet” or “no.” If you’re unsure, you don’t have to answer right away. You might say:.

“I care about you, and I need some time before I know what this looks like.”.

“Can we revisit this in a few months?”.

“I’m not able to be friends right now, and I hope you can respect that.”.

If you’re the one who wants friendship, the kindest move is to respect the space your ex has asked for. If you push for contact, it can get harder for you both to move on, even if giving them room hurts.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cognitive changes may stem from perimenopause, ADHD, or early dementia, each of which requires distinct treatment.
  • Q: How do I know whether hormonal changes related to perimenopause are causing my cognitive function problems, or my ADHD is getting worse, or I might be experiencing mild cognitive impairment or early dementia?
  • According to recent reports, ADHD and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) exhibit clinically different cognitive deficits that help me differentiate one from the other.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cognitive changes may stem from perimenopause, ADHD, or early dementia, each of which requires distinct treatment.

Q: How do I know whether hormonal changes related to perimenopause are causing my cognitive function problems, or my ADHD is getting worse, or I might be experiencing mild cognitive impairment or early dementia?

According to recent reports, ADHD and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) exhibit clinically different cognitive deficits that help me differentiate one from the other. While ADHD symptoms involve forgetfulness, inattention, and distractibility, MCI has specific cognitive symptoms of word-finding challenges, misspellings, and the use of generic terms like “stuff” and “things” because of word-finding difficulty. Also, MCI is progressive over two to three years, whereas ADHD doesn’t generally worsen.

In perimenopause, a decline in estrogen leads to cognitive difficulties. In contrast to MCI, we know that the cognitive changes from estrogen decline are not the result of neurodegeneration.

However, the specific deficits related to declining estrogen haven’t been well differentiated from those associated with ADHD. So if you have pre-existing ADHD and you experience heightened cognitive difficulties in perimenopause and menopause, you may think, “My ADHD is getting worse.” But it’s likely not worsening ADHD. It’s declining estrogen.

It has been revealed that okay, so what do you do about it? There is a paucity of research for clinical guidance. Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) was not always recommended because it was alleged to increase risk for breast cancer and other illnesses. That claim has now been refuted by the most recent research, which has led to the removal of the black box warning from the FDA on HRT product labels. And so, if I have a female patient with ADHD who is 50 years old and says, “For the past two years, I’ve had cognitive decline,” the question to consider is this: “Do I increase her stimulant medication or do I put her on HRT?”.

It has been revealed that I am inclined at that point to put her on HRT for three months, keep her stimulant medication dosage stable, and monitor the qualitative changes in her cognitive functioning. If there is improvement on HRT, then the question becomes, “Does she stay on HRT for some extended period of time along with the stimulant medication?” If the HRT doesn’t work or she can’t take HRT for medical reasons, then I might increase the stimulant medication dosage to see if we can’t overcome the perimenopausal changes from the estrogen decline. This advice comes from my clinical experience, and it is unfortunate that we don’t have more research for clinical guidance here.

[Take This Self-Test: Is It Perimenopause or ADHD?].

Q: Could ADHD stimulant medication mask symptoms of mild cognitive impairment?

There is very limited research on stimulants and mild cognitive impairment (MCI). My clinical impression is that stimulants likely improve symptoms of MCI, but do not take that as an endorsement to seek treatment for MCI with stimulants. There is emerging research on MCI and stimulants that has not yet been published. The follow-up question to that is, if you have ADHD and MCI, will treating the ADHD delay the development of MCI or Alzheimer’s? There is no clinical research for me to answer that question. But if this were me, I’d be treating my ADHD, keeping my fingers crossed, and appreciating the fact that the quality of my life on medicine is better than it would be without my ADHD treated.

Q: Does ADHD get worse as you get older?

In a recent development, ADHD should not get worse; however, the experience of ADHD may be worse if life’s demands start to increase and exceed your ability to compensate. However, if you’re having cognitive changes that are beyond the scope of your ADHD, you may have two neurologic processes going on: your ADHD and something else. In this case, your ADHD may, indeed, be getting worse because you have a second neurological process that needs to be evaluated.

David W. Goodman, M.D., is an internationally recognized expert on adult ADHD.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Certain personality traits may help explain why some people betray a partner’s trust.

Certain personality traits may help explain why some people betray a partner’s trust.

Psychopathy, manipulativeness and narcissism are all associated with cheating.

The strongest average link is with psychopathy, closely followed by Machiavellianism.

Narcissism, which involves an inflated sense of self-importance and a need for admiration, has the weakest link.

Impulsivity, emotional coldness and a willingness to manipulate others may help explain why these characteristics are associated with betrayal.

The conclusions come from a review of 11 studies examining dark personality traits and infidelity.

Participants included university students, married couples and adults from the general population.

All three traits were positively associated with infidelity, although the strength of the association varied between studies.

Psychopathic traits include impulsivity, low empathy and a lack of guilt.

Someone with these characteristics may be more drawn to immediate sexual rewards and less concerned about hurting a partner.

A willingness to take risks could also make the possibility of being caught less of a deterrent — impulsivity and deception may help explain this link.

Psychopathy had the largest average correlation with cheating, although its association was close to that of Machiavellianism.

Machiavellianism involves a cynical view of others and a willingness to manipulate people for personal advantage.

In romantic relationships, these characteristics could make deception easier to justify when it serves someone’s interests.

However, a calculating approach may also encourage caution.

Someone concerned with protecting their reputation might weigh the potential rewards of an affair against the consequences of discovery.

This calculated approach could help explain Machiavellianism’s slightly weaker link with cheating.

Narcissism involves feelings of superiority, entitlement and a strong desire for admiration.

Attention from another potential partner may appeal to someone who places great importance on being desirable.

Nevertheless, narcissism had the smallest average association with infidelity and produced a less consistent pattern across the reviewed studies.

An inflated ego alone therefore offers relatively little information about whether someone has been unfaithful.

The broader picture may depend on how personality combines with relationship satisfaction, commitment and access to alternative partners.

Dark traits provide only part of the explanation for why people betray a partner’s trust.

The study was published in the journal Psihologija (Ataman & Yalçınkaya Alkar, 2025).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Start with an honest conversation that acknowledges the effects of your ADHD on your partner and explains how it thwarts your efforts to be the best possible spouse .”.

Q: “How can I help my husband understand my ADHD so he’s not just complaining all the time about how hard this is for him?”.

Recent findings suggest that first, begin by acknowledging the truth of what he is saying: Your ADHD does, indeed, have tangible effects on him. It also has emotional effects; he likely burns much more mental energy than you can see worrying about whether you completed agreed-upon tasks.

Let down your guard for an honest conversation about the impact of your actions (or inaction) on him. Show him that he matters to you and that you empathize with his experience. You may need to spend significant time here; don’t move on until you’re positive that he really feels that you get it.

[Get This Free Download: Manage ADHD’s Impact on Your Relationship].

Industry observers note that this sets the stage for the second part of the conversation — how ADHD thwarts your efforts to be the best possible partner. In other words, you have good intentions, even if they aren’t obvious, and you can feel equally frustrated and disappointed by what makes him upset. Also, your ADHD makes your life harder, not just his. While his complaints might be accurate, his too-frequent criticisms are not helping.

Finally, discuss how you can work together to address your hotspots. Ask: What can each of us do, or at least try to do, differently to smooth out some of our pain points? For example, do you want reminders? If so, how and when? Also, does he want to give those reminders?

Recent findings suggest that it’s also helpful to discuss protocols when things don’t go according to strategy. How and when can he bring up his concerns in a way that you can hear without getting defensive? How can you tell him that his proposed solution is not working for you?

Encourage your partner to focus on their experience rather than dissecting your actions and making declarations about why you did something.

For example, it’s more effective to say, “It stresses me out when you don’t follow through on commitments because then I feel like I have to take over, and I really don’t want to keep doing that,” versus saying, “You don’t worry about doing things because you know I’ll just do it if you don’t.”.

[Download: 5 Ways to Improve Emotional Control at Home].

I often recommend focusing your conversations on what you want in the future, not what happened in the past.
