  • Coordinating the simultaneous motion of an arm, hand, head, and lips to sip a spoonful of soup feels effortless to the human brain, yet executing such fluid multi-part actions remains one of the most formidable challenges in robotics and computational neuroscience.
  • For decades, neuroscientists have understood that the primary motor cortex (M1) contains an orderly somatotopic “body map”, a spatial arrangement in which distinct cortical zones control individual muscles and body parts, such as a single finger or toe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Neuroscientists discovered a previously hidden full-body map within the secondary motor cortex (M2), a brain region long thought to lack somatotopic organization. The study used high-speed wide-field optical imaging to analyze resting-state brain activity in mice, revealing synchronized sub-regions linking M2 to the sensory cortex that activate during complex, multi-limb actions.

Coordinating the simultaneous motion of an arm, hand, head, and lips to sip a spoonful of soup feels effortless to the human brain, yet executing such fluid multi-part actions remains one of the most formidable challenges in robotics and computational neuroscience.

For decades, neuroscientists have understood that the primary motor cortex (M1) contains an orderly somatotopic “body map”, a spatial arrangement in which distinct cortical zones control individual muscles and body parts, such as a single finger or toe.

However, direct electrical stimulation of the neighboring secondary motor cortex (M2) yielded ambiguous results, leading researchers to conclude that M2 lacked a structured body map and instead operated purely as an abstract motor planning center.

It has been revealed that now, in a study published in Nature Communications, researchers led by Dr. Weihao Xu and Dr. Elizabeth Hillman at Columbia’s Mortimer B. Zuckerman Mind Brain Behavior Institute have overturned that assumption.

Using advanced wide-field optical neuroimaging, the team discovered a complete, previously hidden body map embedded within the resting-state neural activity of M2, revealing how the brain integrates sensory feedback to orchestrate complex, multi-limb movements.

In a recent development, studying motor control in mice poses a unique experimental hurdle because rodents rarely move a single body part in isolation. Rather than relying solely on artificial electrical stimulation or isolated movement tasks, Dr. Xu and colleagues utilized high-speed wide-field optical imaging techniques pioneered in the Hillman laboratory to capture cortex-wide neural dynamics in real time.

Unexpectedly, the critical breakthrough emerged not while the mice were actively moving, but while they were completely at rest. By analyzing spontaneous, seemingly random neural fluctuations across the resting cortex, the investigators spotted localized patches within M2 whose firing patterns synchronized precisely with established body-part sub-regions in the sensory cortex.

“We put these small spots together, and found that they formed a body map hidden in the intrinsic chatter of M2, a part of the brain that wasn’t supposed to have a body map,” said lead author Dr. Weihao Xu, who conducted the research as a doctoral student and postdoctoral scientist in Hillman’s lab.

To ensure these signals were not bleeding over from neighboring M1, Xu spent three years validating the finding using two-color wide-field optical mapping. By optically separating corticospinal projection neurons (which concentrate heavily in M1 and send direct commands down the spinal cord) from surrounding cortical populations, the team confirmed that the newly mapped zones resided squarely within M2.

Anatomical circuit tracing further confirmed that each sub-region of the newfound M2 body map maintained direct structural wiring with its corresponding counterpart in the sensory cortex.

According to recent reports, when the researchers monitored these exact M2 zones during active behaviors, the functional purpose of this hidden map became clear. When a mouse performed a coordinated, multi-part action, such as raising both forepaws toward its mouth while simultaneously licking them, the corresponding forepaw, mouth, and tongue zones within the M2 map lit up together in intense, coordinated bursts.

Industry observers note that “All of these features of M2 explain why understanding the activity patterns of M2 has been so challenging,” said corresponding author Dr. Elizabeth Hillman, now chair of the Department of Imaging Sciences at St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital. “Confusingly, M2 chatters when the body is still, and cares more about complicated movements than simple ones.”.

By revealing how M2 bridges sensory maps with multi-limb motor execution, the findings offer a foundational biological blueprint for understanding how the brain prepares and updates complex actions from moment to moment.

“This newfound map could help researchers understand key details about the dextrous movements that can be lost after brain injuries such as strokes,” Xu noted, adding that decoding how resting-state cortical chatter reflects underlying structural wiring opens fresh avenues for assessing circuit integrity after neurological trauma.

Beyond clinical neurorehabilitation and movement disorders, deciphering how biological brains effortlessly synchronize dozens of joints and sensory streams provides an architectural template for engineers designing next-generation, dexterous autonomous robots.

How does the secondary motor cortex (M2) differ from the primary motor cortex (M1)?

The primary motor cortex (M1) sends direct signals down the spinal cord to control simple, isolated movements of individual body parts. In contrast, the secondary motor cortex (M2) specializes in orchestrating complex, coordinated movements that require multiple body parts to work together simultaneously, such as bringing a cup to your lips.

How did researchers discover the hidden body map in M2?

Instead of relying on traditional electrical stimulation, researchers used high-speed wide-field optical imaging to watch brain activity while mice were resting. They discovered small patches in M2 whose spontaneous resting activity synchronized with known body-part regions in the sensory cortex, forming a complete, previously undetected map.

Why is this discovery crucial for stroke recovery and robotics?

Understanding how M2 maps and coordinates multi-limb movements helps neuroscientists pinpoint why complex dexterity is lost after strokes or brain injuries, potentially guiding targeted neurorehabilitation. It also gives robotics engineers a biological blueprint for programming fluid, multi-joint coordination.

According to recent reports, funding: Funding for this work was provided by National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke BRAIN Initiative grants U19NS104649, R01 NS076628, R01 NS063226 and UM1NS132358 National Institute of Mental Health BRAIN Initiative grants RF1 MH114276 and RF1MH128969, the Simons Collaboration on the Global Brain grant 542991 and Foundation Leducq grant 22CVD01, and the American Lebanese Syrian Associated Charities (ALSAC), the fundraising and awareness organization of St. Jude.

Intrinsic Neural Dynamics Reveal a Body-Part-Specific Topography in Mouse Secondary Motor Cortex.

According to recent reports, the mammalian sensory cortex (S1) has a well-characterized body part-specific topography. However, most motor cortex atlases to date are only coarsely defined.

Here, we demonstrate that optical mapping of neuronal activity in awake mice reveals a distinct, body-part specific organization of mouse secondary motor cortex (M2).

Sources indicate that this M2 topography was identified by recognizing that intrinsic neuronal fluctuations are selectively synchronized between homologous sub-regions of S1 and M2. These fluctuations were strongest during rest and quenched during movement, and were not prominent in corticospinal neurons (CSNs), indicating that they do not represent motor output.

Functional characterization of M2 sub-regions during spontaneous movements confirms body-part specificity, and stronger engagement during multi-effector coordinated actions. Structural connectivity atlas tracings from S1 regions confirm projections to homologous M2 sub-regions.

These results reveal an key underlying topography within M2, and demonstrate intrinsic neuronal dynamics as a window into the functional architecture of the motor cortex.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Urogdy and his classmates also found that Gen Z, which is the cohort born between 1997 and 2012 and considered the first true “digital natives,” is more comfortable than their elders in having a political conversation online—findings that suggest they may be more reachable and receptive to online interventions aimed at reducing polarization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that polarization is a fact of political life in the U.S. today. Gen Z, however, is less inclined than older generations to view it as a permanent fixture in American politics, according to research by students in the Stanford political science course Democracy in the Balance: Polarization and the Road Ahead. Students found that Gen Z is more optimistic than any other age group about the possibility of bridging the political divide in America.

Recent findings suggest that “Polarization doesn’t seem to be a fixed trend in Gen Z’s minds,” remarked Jadon Urogdy. “We have a bright future. Our identities and views are still malleable, and that’s exactly why this moment matters so much.”.

Urogdy and his classmates also found that Gen Z, which is the cohort born between 1997 and 2012 and considered the first true “digital natives,” is more comfortable than their elders in having a political conversation online—findings that suggest they may be more reachable and receptive to online interventions aimed at reducing polarization.

Urogdy’s results were among many findings from Democracy in the Balance: Polarization and the Road Ahead, a spring quarter course taught by Ashley Fabrizio, a Stanford alum and head of research at the nonpartisan think tank More in Common. Working with Fabrizio and her team, students created and conducted a nationally representative survey of 1,610 U.S. adults that oversampled Gen Z to provide a more granular look into their political attitudes and opinions.

Fabrizio, who has taught the course for three years, has found that working with students surfaces concerns that standard polling may miss. “If we want to know what Gen Z’s political beliefs and attitudes are, we should let our students, as members of Gen Z, use their intuition to decide what matters in a survey,” Fabrizio explained.

Working in small groups, students were allocated several minutes of survey time to explore topics such as the political influence of online content promoting masculinity—aka the “manosphere”—the religious revival in Gen Z’s lives, and their beliefs about the American dream. Fabrizio guided students step by step through survey design, showing them how to craft research questions, field the survey, analyze data, and, finally, present their findings.

Students also examined the academic literature on polarization’s effects in American politics, such as how it contributes to political gridlock, drives support for political violence, and erodes trust in American institutions.

“There are many legitimate divisions in politics over competing policies and values, but polarization often drives us apart unnecessarily,” said Fabrizio. “Young Americans will have to find their own ways of bridging partisan differences and overcoming misconceptions about one another. I hope this class helps students see the value of doing so and gives them a sense of agency in addressing polarization.”.

In a recent development, natalia Galperin was excited about the opportunity to run her own study from start to finish, a first for the Stanford undergrad majoring in psychology. She also wanted to expand on her prior work as a research assistant for political scientist Shanto Iyengar in his Political Communication Lab, where she studied the effects of negative political campaign ads.

For her research project, Galperin examined the role of social media in inflating Gen Z’s hostility toward people from the opposing political party, a phenomenon political scientists call “affective polarization.”.

“We thought Gen Z would be more polarized and misinformed because we get so much of our news on social media compared to older generations,” Galperin said.

What she and her classmates found reveals a more complicated picture.

While Gen Z respondents who noted they used social media daily or almost daily were more likely to dislike the opposing party, their scores were almost identical to those of other generations.

“We found that greater social media engagement is generally linked to more polarized views of political parties, and the effect is seen at similar rates across all generations, not just Gen Z,” said Galperin, who will be interning with More In Common this summer.

Practices to help campus communities connect across lines of race, faith, ideology, and more.

Galperin also wanted to know whether social media deepens the divide between what Gen Z thinks people from the other side believe versus what they actually think, a phenomenon known as “perception gaps.” In testing people’s perceptions on immigration, she found that Gen Z did not appear to hold wildly distorted views about the other side—findings that push back against the familiar narrative that being online warps a person’s perceptions of politics.

Taken together, actively using social media seems to harden Gen Z’s feelings more than it distorts basic facts.

The class also found a wide range of political viewpoints, including differences between Gen Z who identified as Democrats and Republicans.

For example, in Urogdy’s project, he and his teammates found that those who were the most confident that polarization can be reduced identified as conservatives and Republicans, while liberals and Democrats believed the opposite—a finding that Urogdy noted tracks with prior research: A person’s view of government depends on whether or not their political party is in control.

Galperin’s team also found lower levels of affective polarization among Republicans and Gen Z overall, and Democrats who reported actively using social media daily have higher perception gaps on immigration-related problems than average.

Another student team’s project revealed further complexities. They found that many Gen Z respondents are more likely than other generations to attribute problems like the affordability crisis to systemic failures in democracy itself rather than to specific policies or leaders. In their data, a notable share of young people mentioned the system itself “is not capable of doing its job,” signaling a deeper, structural disillusionment.

In a recent development, “I think we’re all exhausted by the political system,” Urogdy stated. “There’s this underlying feeling that what we want isn’t being translated into tangible change, and I think that there’s this overall feeling that instead of having animosity towards people across the aisle, there’s an animosity towards the system itself.”.

Urogdy is pragmatic about what comes next.

“We can’t say polarization will disappear if we will it away,” said Urogdy, who is majoring in political science. Now, he feels he has a better understanding of what kinds of solutions matter. If people are disillusioned with the system, surface-level fixes—such as messaging—won’t last, he said. Efforts need to be ongoing. “If Gen Z is still one of the most reachable generations, the answer is sustained civic engagement, where we can rebuild trust in the system while working to reform it. We have a long path ahead,” said Urogdy, who said he is optimistic.

Fabrizio, too, is hopeful. “Gen Z is inheriting a polarized nation, but they are inheriting deep wells of democratic vitality, as well,” Fabrizio stated. “America has a long history of self-government, a robust civil society, and communities that remain deeply committed to democratic values. Gen Z has high standards for our democracy, but living up to them is within reach. I hope older generations will listen and be inspired by Gen Z’s vision for the American dream.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A newly introduced study brings together 26 labs across the US and Europe to quantify the exact metabolic cost of neural computation. Over a 10-year initiative, researchers will investigate how energy constraints shape brain circuits and behavior, solving mysteries such as why active brains shift toward fast, inefficient glycolysis and how glia and neuromodulators support neurons during intense cognitive demand or oxygen deprivation.

Source: Boston University / Simons Foundation.

Constructing a house without knowing the cost of materials, labor, or individual rooms would make architectural planning impossible. Yet for decades, neuroscientists attempting to decode how the brain processes information have operated without a quantitative metabolic blueprint. While researchers have mapped neural wiring and electrical firing patterns in exquisite detail, the exact energetic cost of thought, how much fuel the brain produces, distributes, and burns to execute specific computations, has remained largely unquantified.

To establish this foundational accounting, the Simons Foundation has launched the Simons Collaboration on Brain Energetics (SCOBE), an ambitious, decade-long international consortium uniting 26 laboratories across the United States and Europe.

Co-led by Dr. Anna Devor, professor of biomedical engineering at Boston University College of Engineering, and Dr. Tom Clandinin, professor of neurobiology at Stanford University, the initiative seeks to determine how strict bioenergetic limits govern neural computation from individual molecules up to whole-brain behavior.

Recent findings suggest that “There are lots of really cool energetics questions, but most of them are completely unanswered,” explained Dr. Devor, whose Boston University laboratory will receive $3.2 million over the next ten years as part of the program. “For example, nobody understands how the brain’s computational principles are constrained by the availability of energetic resources and how that works.”.

Every electrical impulse, synaptic release, and molecular pump in the central nervous system runs on adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the universal energy currency of living cells. Despite its fundamental role, neurobiology lacks a precise mathematical ledger detailing how much ATP different types of neural networks require to store memories, process sensory inputs, or make decisions.

Sources indicate that “Energetics is everything,” Devor emphasized. “Our basic brain activity cannot happen unless the brain utilizes ATP, and we don’t really understand and don’t have a quantitative account of how much ATP different types of computations in the brain utilize.”.

Recent findings suggest that one of the central mysteries SCOBE investigators will tackle is a metabolic shift known as aerobic glycolysis. Under baseline resting conditions, brain cells burn glucose efficiently using oxygen inside mitochondria—the cell’s high-yield power stations. However, the moment neurons become actively engaged in a demanding cognitive task, the brain abruptly begins consuming far more sugar than can be oxidized by mitochondria, routing glucose through rapid, mitochondria-independent glycolysis.

Devor highlights two primary hypotheses driving this phenomenon:.

“These ideas are not new, but testing it experimentally requires new research tools and quantitative models. Our SCOBE consortium is perfectly positioned to deliver both,” Devor noted.

Sources indicate that furthermore, the team will investigate the upstream chemical switches that turn up this metabolic dial during moments of focus and alertness. Researchers suspect that norepinephrine, a neuromodulator closely related to adrenaline that heightens arousal and cognitive acuity, directly triggers rapid glycolysis upregulation to meet sudden computational loads.

It has been revealed that because the brain lacks substantial internal fuel reserves, it depends on continuous vascular delivery of glucose and oxygen. Consequently, even microscopic disruptions, such as blood flow stoppages in single capillaries, can starve local neurons. Such capillary dysfunction and silent microstrokes are pervasive features of biological aging and neurodegenerative disorders like Alzheimer’s disease.

Paradoxically, clinical and experimental studies have also documented remarkable instances where neurons recover full cellular function following prolonged periods of oxygen deprivation, suggesting the brain possesses hidden metabolic survival mechanisms that remain poorly understood.

Unraveling these residual metabolic pathways could yield major breakthroughs in emergency medicine, guiding improved neuroprotective protocols for resuscitation following cardiac arrest or acute ischemic stroke.

Backed by the Simons Foundation’s 10-year funding horizon, double the duration of standard federal grants, and dedicated high-performance computational infrastructure to share massive neurophotonic imaging datasets across partner labs in the U.S., Norway, and Austria, SCOBE aims to build the first comprehensive energetic blueprint of the thinking brain.

What is the Simons Collaboration on Brain Energetics (SCOBE)?

According to recent reports, SCOBE is a 10-year international research consortium comprising 26 labs across the US and Europe, co-led by Anna Devor (Boston University) and Tom Clandinin (Stanford University). Its goal is to quantify the exact energy (ATP) costs of brain computation from the molecular level up to complex behavior.

Why does the brain switch to inefficient energy production when thinking hard?

Recent findings suggest that during active cognitive tasks, the brain consumes extra sugar using glycolysis, a process that yields less ATP per sugar molecule than mitochondria, but operates much faster. Researchers are testing whether the brain trades efficiency for speed, or whether supportive glial cells consume this sugar to fuel active neurons.

How could mapping brain energetics improve medical treatments?

Understanding how brain cells produce energy and survive temporary oxygen shortages could lead to better treatments for stroke, microvascular aging, and neurodegenerative diseases, while improving emergency resuscitation strategies after cardiac arrest.

#10322. Breaking: Scientists restore a brain protein and reverse signs of aging in mice

Breaking: Scientists restore a brain protein and reverse signs of aging in mice

📅 18 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1545 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Memory problems, thinning skin, and declining bone mass may seem like separate consequences of growing older.
  • The findings came from a study published on March 16, 2023, in the open access journal PLOS Biology, led by Lige Leng of Xiamen University in Xiamen, China, and colleagues.
  • The researchers focused on the hypothalamus, a small brain region that helps coordinate metabolism and other essential functions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Memory problems, thinning skin, and declining bone mass may seem like separate consequences of growing older. Yet experiments in mice suggest that changes in a protein deep inside the brain can influence all three. Restoring that protein, called Menin, improved several signs of aging, while a separate treatment with the amino acid D-serine improved cognition.

The findings came from a study published on March 16, 2023, in the open access journal PLOS Biology, led by Lige Leng of Xiamen University in Xiamen, China, and colleagues. The work identified a possible connection between brain inflammation, metabolism, and aging throughout the body. Research published since then has added to that picture, while also showing why the supplement findings require careful interpretation.

How a Brain Protein Could Influence Aging.

The researchers focused on the hypothalamus, a small brain region that helps coordinate metabolism and other essential functions. It also appears to influence how the body ages. As inflammatory signaling increases in this region, it can contribute to changes both within the brain and in tissues elsewhere in the body.

Before the 2023 study, Leng and colleagues had found that Menin helps restrain inflammation in the hypothalamus. That raised an important question: Could losing some of this protection help set age-related decline in motion?

In a recent development, the team found that Menin levels fell with age in certain neurons within the ventromedial hypothalamus, an area involved in regulating metabolism. The same decline was not seen in astrocytes and microglia, two types of cells that support and protect the brain. This suggested that the change was specific to particular cells rather than a uniform loss across the region.

To investigate whether Menin loss could actually contribute to aging, rather than simply accompany it, the researchers created conditional knockout mice. These animals were genetically engineered so that Menin could be selectively removed. Reducing Menin in younger mice increased hypothalamic inflammation and brought on several aging-related traits, including lower bone mass, thinner skin, cognitive decline, and a modestly shorter lifespan.

In a recent development, menin loss also disrupted a chemical pathway crucial for communication between brain cells. Mice with less Menin had lower levels of D-serine, an amino acid that helps activate receptors involved in learning and memory. These receptors help neurons adjust the strength of their connections, a process essential for storing information.

According to recent reports, an enzyme involved in D-serine production (which was in turn regulated by Menin) became less active, reducing the amino acid's supply. The findings suggested that Menin could influence cognition not only through inflammation, but also by helping maintain the chemistry that supports brain signaling.

It has been revealed that D-serine is sometimes used as a dietary supplement, but an crucial distinction can get lost in discussions of food sources. Serine occurs in foods such as soybeans, eggs, fish, and nuts, while the form incorporated into dietary proteins is L-serine. The body can convert L-serine into D-serine, but the two forms are not interchangeable, and eating these foods is not equivalent to receiving the experimental D-serine treatment.

Sources indicate that the researchers next tested whether raising Menin levels could improve the condition of elderly (20-month-old) mice. They delivered the gene for Menin into the hypothalamus, allowing cells in that region to produce more of the protein.

Thirty days later, the treated mice had improvements in skin thickness and bone mass, along with better performance on tests of learning, cognition, and balance. The changes were accompanied by higher D-serine levels in the hippocampus, a brain region essential for learning and memory. The study also reported that restoring Menin extended lifespan in the treated mice.

In a recent development, A separate experiment tested a simpler approach: giving mice D-serine in their drinking water for three weeks. This improved cognitive performance, including in older animals. However, the supplement did not reproduce the broader improvements in physical aging traits seen after Menin restoration. The distinction matters: the study did not show that taking D-serine reversed aging throughout the body.

At the time, Leng described the potential significance of the findings:.

According to recent reports, "We speculate that the decline of Menin expression in the hypothalamus with age may be one of the driving factors of aging, and Menin may be the key protein connecting the genetic, inflammatory, and metabolic factors of aging. D-serine is a potentially promising therapeutic for cognitive decline.".

Leng added, "Ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) Menin signaling diminished in aged mice, which contributes to systemic aging phenotypes and cognitive deficits. The effects of Menin on aging are mediated by neuroinflammatory changes and metabolic pathway signaling, accompanied by serine deficiency in VMH, while restoration of Menin in VMH reversed aging-related phenotypes.".

Subsequent studies have explored related mechanisms, although they should not be treated as direct confirmation of the entire Menin aging pathway.

A study published in the Journal of Physiology and Biochemistry in March 2024 examined Menin in cultured mouse hippocampal cells exposed to the stress hormone corticosterone. A compound called itaconate increased Menin levels and reduced inflammation and a form of cell death. When the researchers silenced Menin, that protection disappeared. The result supported a protective role for Menin in another experimental setting, but it was a cell study, not a demonstration of slower aging in animals or people.

Other work has strengthened the case that communication between the hypothalamus and the rest of the body can influence aging. In a 2024 Cell Metabolism study, researchers at Washington University School of Medicine identified a different group of hypothalamic neurons that communicates with fat tissue. Interventions that maintained or stimulated this system increased physical activity and extended lifespan in mice. The study involved a different molecular pathway from Menin, but reinforced the broader idea that brain signals can affect aging beyond the brain.

Recent findings suggest that A much larger view emerged in January 2025, when an Allen Institute team reported an analysis of roughly 1.2 million mouse brain cells in Nature. Some of the cell types most sensitive to aging were concentrated around the hypothalamus's third ventricle, a fluid-filled cavity. Many showed reduced activity in genes associated with neuronal function alongside increased activity in genes related to immune responses. That study mapped changes associated with aging rather than testing a treatment, but it highlighted the hypothalamus as an crucial area for further investigation.

Why More D-Serine Is Not Necessarily Better.

Later research also complicates the idea that increasing D-serine should always benefit an aging brain.

Industry observers note that in April 2025, a study in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences examined mice engineered to develop features of Alzheimer's disease. In that model, an early rise in D-serine accompanied disruptions in brain signaling. Genetically removing the enzyme that produces D-serine prevented or reduced several later cognitive problems. This was a different biological setting from the Menin experiments, but it demonstrated that D-serine can have different effects depending on the underlying disease process.

Research published on September 16, 2026, in the Journal of Alzheimer's Disease pointed in another direction. In a different Alzheimer's mouse model, a diet enriched with L-serine increased blood levels of both L-serine and D-serine and partially restored measures of latest neuron production in the hippocampus. It did not improve the buildup of amyloid, a protein associated with Alzheimer's disease. Importantly, this experiment tested L-serine and the production of new neurons, not D-serine supplementation as a treatment for human aging.

According to recent reports, taken together, these findings suggest that serine metabolism is a promising research target, but not a simple case of more being better. The form of serine, the condition being studied, and the outcome being measured all matter. Neither study directly confirms or overturns the original Menin results.

What the Findings Mean for People.

There is some human research on D-serine, although it does not establish an aging treatment. A small randomized study published in 2016, before the Menin work, tested a single dose in 50 healthy older adults. Participants improved on one measure of a computerized maze task, but the researchers found no significant benefit on the other cognitive tests or mood measures. The experiment did not establish lasting memory benefits, slower aging, or the safety of prolonged use in older adults.

The Menin findings leave several important questions unresolved. Researchers still need to determine what causes the protein to decline with age, how much of the resulting physical and cognitive deterioration can be prevented, and how long any benefits might last. They also need to understand whether altering Menin or supplementing D-serine could produce unintended effects.

The central possibility remains compelling: some changes associated with aging may be influenced by signals originating in a small part of the brain. Understanding those signals could reveal ways to protect function later in life. For now, however, the evidence points to an experimental pathway worth investigating, not a supplement proven to turn back human aging.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Track pants, also known as tracksuit bottoms, receive the lower ratings for perceived intelligence compared with blouses, ordinary trousers or long skirts in a study of women’s clothing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One everyday garment came last for both perceived intelligence and trustworthiness.

One everyday garment came last for both perceived intelligence and trustworthiness.

Track pants, also known as tracksuit bottoms, receive the lower ratings for perceived intelligence compared with blouses, ordinary trousers or long skirts in a study of women’s clothing.

Of the six types of clothing the researchers compared, track pants also received the lowest average ratings for trustworthiness.

Blouses topped the rankings for intelligence and trustworthiness but scored near the bottom for confidence.

Short skirts showed almost the reverse pattern, scoring near the top for confidence and lower than long skirts on both intelligence and trustworthiness.

Short skirts also gave the strongest impression of sexual interest, showing how much people can read into a hemline.

Long skirts fell between short skirts and blouses on confidence, while ordinary trousers scored higher than tracksuit bottoms on both intelligence and trustworthiness.

Onesies gave the strongest impression of happiness and scored about as high as short skirts for confidence.

White clothes suggested a happier wearer than grey clothes did, with black clothes coming last.

These examples show how the impression changes with the question being asked: a blouse came out ahead for intelligence, while a onesie came out ahead for happiness.

The researchers began by asking about 200 people what they thought clothes could tell them about someone and comparing their answers with traits examined in previous research.

They then gathered ratings on 5,000 photographs from online shops, covering five kinds of impressions: intelligence, confidence, trustworthiness, happiness and sexual interest.

Participants formed these impressions from photographs of the garments alone, without seeing anyone wearing them.

The results showed that who was doing the judging explained more of the variation in ratings than which garment they saw.

For example, one person might associate tracksuit bottoms with training for a race, while another might picture someone spending a Sunday on the sofa.

The researchers draw a parallel between judging people by their clothes and judging them by their faces:.

“That is, much like inferences from faces, the inferred attributes often lie in the eye of the beholder.”.

The study was published in the Journal of Computational Social Science (Rosenbusch et al., 2021).

Industry News: The Overlooked Ways Love Indicates Up in Urban Spaces

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1132 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, over the past two decades, my doctoral students and I have focused on studying love, care, kindness, and compassion in urban settings.
  • It has been revealed that but, as someone who has lived and worked in large urban centers—Latest York City, Chicago, Detroit, Istanbul—I know firsthand that urban centers are also sites of human virtue.
  • My former students and I have been eager to understand how love, generosity, and care manifest and operate in the hyperdiverse, densely populated, loud, fast-paced complexities of urban spaces.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, over the past two decades, my doctoral students and I have focused on studying love, care, kindness, and compassion in urban settings. Why? Because social science research on life in America’s cities is desperately incomplete. Much like the vision of urban life that permeates most of American popular culture, social science research imagines urban areas as sites of overwhelmedness, disengagement, social and moral crisis, threat, and violence.

It has been revealed that but, as someone who has lived and worked in large urban centers—Latest York City, Chicago, Detroit, Istanbul—I know firsthand that urban centers are also sites of human virtue. People in urban contexts, including those living in high-stress, oversurveilled, underresourced communities, draw daily from deep wells of love, compassion, empathy, kindness, and generosity in the service of caring for each other. From holding doors open for one another, to offering seats on buses and trains, to stopping to help with directions, to paying unexpected compliments, city-dwellers create environments that are saturated with powerful but easily missed acts of care.

My former students and I have been eager to understand how love, generosity, and care manifest and operate in the hyperdiverse, densely populated, loud, fast-paced complexities of urban spaces. Through surveys and interviews, we have sought to understand how adults residing in significant cities define love, how they see love being expressed, and their views of the cascading effects of giving and receiving care, generosity, and love.

In a recent development, we have learned that the decision to express love and care for others in large cities is not simply a moral or emotional decision. We offer two examples of the lens needed to notice the presence of love in cities.

It has been revealed that first, we have learned that identities matter in experiences of compassion, love, and care between strangers. Urban dwellers’ identity (for example, race or gender), lived experience, context, familial, cultural, and legal systems’ realities work together to shape decisions about whether to extend acts of love to people you do not know. For example, Kehinde, a 26-year-old African American man living in a large, densely populated city, described his experience of giving and receiving kindness, care, and love in his city as shaped by how he navigates other people seeing him as a Black man.

Industry observers note that “I will see folks all the time that may need a hand with their bags or crossing the street or just little things like that. And I take a second, hesitate,” Kehinde claims. “I don’t want to scare them. I don’t want to come off as a threat.”.

Industry observers note that to get through these moments, Kehinde describes engaging in a practice of analysis and shape-shifting. Before he steps in to offer help, he assesses the environment and changes the way he carries himself so that people will perceive him as a possible helper rather than as a threat. He says: “I smile a lot more. My voice might change a bit.” He might shrink his body and keep his head down, to avoid seeming intimidating. After helping someone, he moves along without lingering. Reflecting, he acknowledges not being his full, true self in these interactions. “I have to realize I’ve been socialized—made to believe that this is what I need to do in order to navigate the situation.” Kehinde’s story highlights the point that identities matter in economies of care. The images and stereotypes that we construct about people come at a cost even in moments of compassion. Stereotypes affect who we perceive as deserving of care, concern, and protection. Stereotypes also inform our expectations about who can be trusted to help. Stereotyping is not unique to urban settings. But because urban settings tend to be especially diverse spaces, they create abundant opportunities to study how identities and the social scripts we hold affect the way that strangers care for each other across lines of difference. What Kehinde and others bring to the fore is the reality that the targets of stereotyping are aware of the ways that they are perceived. They learn that to be seen as helpful rather than as threatening, they need to read situations correctly, make adjustments to their approaches (e.g., keep “appropriate” distance), and exit situations strategically. Targets of stereotyping must strike a balance between their own deep-seated motivations to behave caringly and their desire to stay safe. For individuals like Kehinde, miscalculations can be costly. If, in the effort to behave lovingly and compassionately, someone is misidentified as a threat, that can lead to a range of consequences from being rebuffed and embarrassed to becoming the target of violence, arrest, or death. The end result is that people consciously or unconsciously learn the rules of engagement around helping strangers.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

Industry observers note that A second lesson that has emerged from studying love in urban settings is that love lives in the built environment of cities. I highlight this lesson in my Positive Psychology in Urban Settings classes. Cities are often saturated with murals, billboards, and symbols that convey messages of love, solidarity, and belonging. As residents move through neighborhood streets, they may encounter signs prominently posted in shop windows or near the entrances of religious institutions that remind them that “Black Lives Matter,” “Love Is Love,” or “Immigrants Are Welcome Here.” People display rainbow flags and national flags from apartment windows, on cars, and in other spaces, declaring both their own identities and pride for and solidarity with those identities. The architecture of urban spaces may also play a role in expressions of love and care. In many urban neighborhoods, porches, stoops, and front steps serve as places of connection and care. Simple greetings (e.g., “Morning, baby!,” “You doing good?”) voiced by neighbors sitting on their steps serve as ways of spatializing love, care, and connection in urban landscapes.

I return here to my initial point. Our studies of urban areas are desperately incomplete and will remain incomplete until we more fully examine how various forms of human goodness—including love and care—flourish in urban settings. Likewise, our understandings of love and care will remain underdeveloped until we explore how these experiences emerge in the most densely populated, diverse, complex social structures in which people live. We will truly understand love when we understand how it is titrated through place, context, history, culture, religion, structures of power, identities, and a host of individual and relational factors. Urban centers give us powerful opportunities to know love.

Jacqueline Mattis, Ph.D., is dean of the School of Arts and Sciences at Rutgers University-Newark. She studies human goodness in urban contexts.

CRISPR Enhancer Editing Rescues Autism Brain Organoids

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1025 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers demonstrated in lab-grown human brain cells and cortical organoids that boosting the activity of a single healthy gene copy can offset the cellular effects of autism-linked genetic mutations.
  • The study used a modified CRISPR technique targeting noncoding DNA enhancers for the CHD8 and SCN2A genes, safely normalizing tissue growth and neuronal electrical firing exclusively in mutated cells without causing toxic gene overexpression.
  • Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) carries a substantial genetic component, with roughly 15% of genetic risk arising from de novo mutations, spontaneous genetic alterations that appear for the first time in a child rather than being inherited.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers demonstrated in lab-grown human brain cells and cortical organoids that boosting the activity of a single healthy gene copy can offset the cellular effects of autism-linked genetic mutations.

The study used a modified CRISPR technique targeting noncoding DNA enhancers for the CHD8 and SCN2A genes, safely normalizing tissue growth and neuronal electrical firing exclusively in mutated cells without causing toxic gene overexpression.

Source: UCLA Health / Nature Neuroscience.

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) carries a substantial genetic component, with roughly 15% of genetic risk arising from de novo mutations, spontaneous genetic alterations that appear for the first time in a child rather than being inherited.

Many of these high-impact mutations result in haploinsufficiency, a biological state in which one copy of a critical developmental gene is disabled, leaving the remaining healthy copy unable to produce enough protein to sustain typical neurodevelopment.

While existing clinical interventions primarily manage behavioral and cognitive symptoms, developing gene therapies to correct the underlying molecular deficits has proven exceptionally challenging, largely because delivering extra copies of large genes or directly overexpressing them can cause severe cellular toxicity.

It has been revealed that now, in a study published in Nature Neuroscience, researchers at UCLA Health led by Dr. Daniel Geschwind and Dr. George Chen have unveiled a precision epigenomic strategy that sidesteps these hurdles.

Working in human stem cell-derived neurons and three-dimensional cortical organoids, the team used a modified CRISPR system to gently turn up the volume on the body’s own remaining healthy gene copy, nudging developing brain cells back toward typical trajectories.

Rather than cutting DNA or inserting synthetic transgenes, the investigators utilized CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) directed at enhancers, specialized stretches of noncoding regulatory DNA that function like biological dimmer dials, dictating precisely when, where, and how strongly a target gene is expressed.

The team focused on two of the most prominent genes linked to autism and neurodevelopmental disorders:.

By targeting endogenous enhancers rather than the gene promoters themselves, the researchers sought to keep gene activation strictly synchronized with natural, cell-type-specific developmental rhythms and prevent dangerous overshooting into gene overexpression.

Sources indicate that “Many autism-linked mutations leave a person with one working copy of a gene instead of two,” explained senior author Dr. Daniel Geschwind, the Gordon and Virginia MacDonald Distinguished Professor of Human Genetics, Neurology, and Psychiatry at UCLA. “Our results show that, in human cell models, it’s possible to turn up that remaining copy and move cells back toward typical development. This is a key first step, and it gives us a latest way to think about addressing the biology underlying these conditions.”.

To test the therapeutic potential of enhancer activation, the researchers engineered human induced pluripotent stem cells carrying CHD8 or SCN2A mutations into two advanced laboratory platforms: two-dimensional cultures of human excitatory neurons and three-dimensional cortical organoids, self-organizing clusters of brain-like tissue that recapitulate early human cortical assembly.

The results demonstrated targeted molecular and functional rescue across both genetic models:.

In a recent development, “What stands out to us is that the approach acted only in cell lines carrying the mutation and left healthy cell lines alone,” noted first author Dr. George Chen, a former postdoctoral fellow in the Geschwind lab and current assistant professor of neurology at Children’s Hospital of Los Angeles. “That kind of specificity matters for any future therapy. We are still a long way from the clinic, and there is a lot of work ahead on delivery and timing, but these findings provide hope and give us a clear direction.”.

The study also revealed that developmental timing plays a decisive role: enhancer activation yielded the strongest cellular rescue when applied during specific developmental windows, underscoring the dynamic nature of chromatin accessibility as neurons mature.

While the authors caution that the work represents an early-stage proof of concept conducted entirely in vitro, and that translating CRISPR enhancer therapies to patients will require overcoming major blood-brain barrier delivery hurdles and establishing efficacy beyond early embryonic windows, the implications extend far beyond CHD8 and SCN2A.

Because hundreds of neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions stem from single-copy gene loss, harnessing the genome’s natural regulatory dials could provide a versatile blueprint for precision molecular medicine.

How does this latest CRISPR approach differ from traditional gene therapy?

Sources indicate that traditional gene therapy often attempts to replace a broken gene or permanently force it to stay switched on, which can cause toxic overexpression. Instead, the UCLA team used a modified CRISPR tool aimed at DNA “enhancers”, natural regulatory switches that control when and how strongly a gene operates, to gently boost the activity of the cell’s existing healthy gene copy within safe biological limits.

What improvements did researchers see in the lab-grown brain models?

It has been revealed that in human cortical organoids with CHD8 mutations, boosting the healthy gene copy reduced abnormal tissue overgrowth and helped neurons mature properly. In neurons with SCN2A mutations, the approach restored normal electrical firing activity.

Why is this treatment considered promising for safety?

Recent findings suggest that the CRISPR enhancer treatment only boosted gene activity in cells carrying the autism-linked mutation, leaving healthy cells and neighboring genes completely unchanged. Because it relies on existing natural gene regulation, it avoids the dangerous side effects of excessive protein production.

Enhancer-targeted CRISPR-A rescues haploinsufficiency and mutant phenotypes in organoid models of autism.

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a highly heritable condition with diverse clinical presentations. Approximately 15% of the genetic susceptibility of ASD is imparted by de novo haploinsufficient mutations of major effect.

We mapped enhancers of two high-confidence autism genes, CHD8 and SCN2A, and used CRISPR-based gene activation targeting enhancers (eCRISPR-A) in human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived excitatory neurons and cerebral forebrain organoids to correct the effects of haploinsufficiency, taking advantage of the presence of a wild-type allele of each gene and endogenous gene regulation.

Here we show that eCRISPR-A induced a sustained increase in CHD8 and SCN2A expression specifically in mutant neurons and cortical organoids, with rescue of gene expression levels and mutation-associated phenotypes, including gene expression and physiology.

These data support gene activation via targeting enhancers of haploinsufficient genes as a therapeutic intervention in ASD and other neurodevelopmental disorders.

Scientists create a needle-thin brain implant that can do three jobs at once

📅 21 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (894 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new type of brain implant could give scientists a more precise way to study the brain and may eventually contribute to treatments for neurological conditions such as epilepsy.
  • Researchers from DTU, the University of Copenhagen, University College London, and other institutions have developed a long, needle-thin brain electrode equipped with microscopic channels.
  • The findings were published in the journal Advanced Science.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new type of brain implant could give scientists a more precise way to study the brain and may eventually contribute to treatments for neurological conditions such as epilepsy.

Researchers from DTU, the University of Copenhagen, University College London, and other institutions have developed a long, needle-thin brain electrode equipped with microscopic channels. Known as the microfluidic Axialtrode (mAxialtrode), the device is designed to provide multiple functional points along the length of the implant. This allows researchers to record neural activity and deliver medication to specific locations across different parts of the brain.

The findings were published in the journal Advanced Science.

A Multifunction Tool for Brain Research.

Sources indicate that for now, the technology is primarily intended as a research tool. Scientists could use it to investigate how signals travel through different layers of the brain during processes involving epilepsy, memory, and decision-making.

Over the longer term, the researchers say the mAxialtrode could also have therapeutic applications. One possibility would be using the device to deliver drugs to precise locations while simultaneously applying electrical stimulation or light stimulation to selected areas of the brain.

Recent findings suggest that postdoc Kunyang Sui, who developed the mAxialtrode concept together with Associate Professor Christos Markos, states one of the main advantages is that several capabilities can be combined within a single implant. That could allow researchers to perform more precise experiments while reducing the need for multiple devices inserted into the brain.

"Most current brain implants are based on hard materials such as silicon, which can irritate the brain and trigger inflammatory reactions in the tissue. The new implant differs in that it is made of soft, plastic-like optical fibers and has a specially angled tip that makes it smaller and reduces the damage caused when it is placed in the brain," states Kunyang Sui.

Industry observers note that sui cautions that the technology is still far from routine clinical use. Extensive testing, additional development, and regulatory approvals would be required before it could be used to treat patients.

Moving Beyond Conventional Optical Fibers.

Brain researchers at the moment use flat-ended optical fibers in many experiments. These thin fibers, made from glass or plastic, can carry light into deep regions of the brain. They are frequently used in optogenetics, a technique in which specific nerve cells are activated using light.

Industry observers note that conventional fibers, however, have an important limitation. They typically interact with brain tissue only at the end of the fiber, meaning researchers can stimulate or monitor just one location at a time.

The outermost end is called the distal tip, or the "nose" of the fiber. Light is emitted and contact with brain tissue occurs only at this point. As a result, scientists may be limited to measuring or stimulating one brain layer at a time, even though many brain functions depend on communication among several layers and deeper structures.

How the New Brain Implant Works.

The needle-thin mAxialtrode begins as a much larger polymer rod. Researchers heat the material and draw it into an extremely thin fiber, somewhat like producing a very fine strand of sugar, but with far greater precision.

In a recent development, A light-conducting core runs through the center of the fiber. Surrounding it are eight microscopic channels that can transport liquids. Those channels can also hold extremely thin metal wires used to measure electrical activity in the brain.

In a recent development, the finished fiber measures less than half a millimeter across. It is also highly flexible, allowing it to move along with brain tissue rather than pressing rigidly through it. This difference in stiffness could be important because harder implants can trigger inflammatory responses when they remain in the brain for long periods.

According to recent reports, the researchers tested the system not only in the laboratory but also "in vivo," meaning in living mice. The electrode was implanted in the animals' brains and connected to light sources, recording equipment, and small pumps used to deliver fluids.

The experiments revealed that the device could stimulate nerve cells using both blue and red light. At the same time, researchers were able to record electrical activity from shallow and deeper brain regions, including the cerebral cortex and hippocampus.

It has been revealed that they were also able to inject different substances at separate depths, with delivery points spaced almost three millimeters apart. All of these measurements and forms of stimulation were carried out using a single lightweight fiber, which the mice were able to carry without any obvious signs of discomfort.

Potential Applications in Epilepsy and Neuroscience.

The in vivo experiments and neurophysiological validation were performed in close collaboration with Associate Professor Rune W. Berg of the University of Copenhagen and Associate Professor Rob C. Wykes from University College London. Their contributions included expertise in analyzing neural circuits and models relevant to epilepsy.

The research team is now working to patent the technology behind the brain electrode. The scientists are also exploring what would be required to begin testing the device in patients within a clinical setting.

Genetic Switch Helped Evolve the Large Primate Brain

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (969 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers discovered a primate-specific DNA regulatory switch that governs the production of specialized brain-building stem cells called basal radial glia (bRG).
  • What genetic innovations enabled the human cerebral cortex, the wrinkled outer sheet of neural tissue responsible for language, abstract reasoning, perception, and memory, to grow vastly larger and more intricate than the brains of most other mammals?
  • For decades, evolutionary neurobiologists have hunted for uniquely human genes that either expand the starting pool of neural progenitor cells or prolong the developmental window during which those cells divide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers discovered a primate-specific DNA regulatory switch that governs the production of specialized brain-building stem cells called basal radial glia (bRG). The study indicates that evolution expanded primate cerebral cortex complexity by altering how the shared DACH1 gene is regulated, boosting bRG progenitor production without needing to invent entirely newly introduced genes.

Source: National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University.

What genetic innovations enabled the human cerebral cortex, the wrinkled outer sheet of neural tissue responsible for language, abstract reasoning, perception, and memory, to grow vastly larger and more intricate than the brains of most other mammals?

For decades, evolutionary neurobiologists have hunted for uniquely human genes that either expand the starting pool of neural progenitor cells or prolong the developmental window during which those cells divide.

Now, a collaborative team of researchers in Taiwan and Japan has uncovered a third evolutionary mechanism: rather than inventing latest genes from scratch, evolution rewrote the regulatory instructions controlling an ancient, shared gene to alter which types of brain-building cells are manufactured.

Led by investigators at National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University (NYCU) and Academia Sinica in Taiwan, alongside collaborators at Kyoto University in Japan, the study pinpoints a small noncoding DNA element that drives the production of basal radial glia (bRG), a specialized class of neural stem cells essential for cortical expansion.

Recent findings suggest that to conceptualize how embryonic brain development evolved, the researchers compare the developing cortex to a biological factory staffed by neural stem cells. Evolution can scale up output by enlarging the workforce or extending factory operating hours, or it can modify the factory’s operating manual to produce a specialized mix of workers.

Sources indicate that in developing primate brains, basal radial glia (bRGs) serve as high-capacity cortical builders. Abundant in humans and non-human primates yet remarkably scarce in rodents, bRGs undergo repeated rounds of self-renewing division within the outer subventricular zone, dramatically amplifying the neuronal output needed to fold and expand the cerebral cortex. They also generate upper-layer projection neurons that form long-range connections bridging distant cortical regions and hemispheres.

Recent findings suggest that “What interested us was that the gene already exists in both humans and mice. The notable difference may not be the gene itself, but the instructions controlling how it is used during brain development. That gives us another way to understand how evolution could produce different kinds of brains,” explained Professor Pei-Shan Hou at the Institute of Anatomy and Cell Biology, NYCU, Taiwan.

According to recent reports, the research team focused on DACH1 (Dachshund Family Transcription Factor 1), a developmental gene conserved across mice, monkeys, and humans. Comparative genomic analysis revealed a compact regulatory DNA sequence acting as an enhancer switch for DACH1; while conserved across primates, this regulatory motif differs in non-primate vertebrates.

To determine how this evolutionary edit shapes cortical assembly, the investigators combined cross-species stem cell engineering with live-tissue neuroimaging:.

Further molecular dissection indicated that DACH1 drives this cell-fate shift by suppressing an opposing signaling pathway that otherwise restricts neural stem cell diversification, ultimately shifting the balance of newborn neurons toward subtypes that wire the brain’s two hemispheres together.

While the authors emphasize that brain evolution and human intelligence emerge from complex, multi-gene networks rather than a single regulatory switch, the findings demonstrate how subtle tweaks in noncoding DNA can profoundly reshape cellular architecture.

By illuminating how regulatory DNA coordinates progenitor identity and developmental timing, the work provides both a clearer framework for understanding primate brain evolution and improved benchmarks for engineering high-fidelity human cortical organoids to model neurodevelopmental disorders.

How did evolution help make the human brain larger without creating new genes?

It has been revealed that researchers discovered that evolution modified a small regulatory stretch of noncoding DNA, acting like a genetic switch, that controls an existing gene called DACH1. By altering when and how strongly DACH1 is used during development, primates produce far more cortex-building stem cells than mice, even though both species share the DACH1 gene.

What are basal radial glia (bRG), and why are they vital?

It has been revealed that basal radial glia are specialized neural stem cells that are abundant in developing primate brains but rare in mice. They divide repeatedly to generate huge numbers of neurons for the cerebral cortex—the brain’s outer layer responsible for memory, language, and complex thought—as well as nerve cells that connect the brain’s two hemispheres.

How did scientists prove this DNA switch controls brain cell production?

In a recent development, when researchers deleted the primate regulatory DNA region from lab-grown human and rhesus monkey brain organoids, the organoids produced significantly fewer basal radial glia cells. Conversely, inserting the human DNA switch into developing mouse brains increased the production of bRG-like cells.

An LHX2-DACH1 regulatory innovation drives basal progenitor expansion in the primate neocortex.

A defining feature of the primate neocortex is an expanded cortical progenitor pool, especially the basal radial glia (bRG), contributing to complex intracortical circuitry underlying higher cognition.

Here, a comparative transcriptomic analysis of developing human and mouse neocortical cells identified DACH1 as a transcription factor enriched in human neurogenic RGs.

Recent findings suggest that using both primate ESCs and mouse models, we found an LHX2-DACH1-miR-215-5p program regulating bRG production. DACH1 loss in human cortical progenitors impaired bRG production and shifted neuronal output toward corticospinal neurons, whereas Dach1 depletion in mice had no effect.

Conversely, ectopic DACH1 expression in the rodent neocortex induced bRG formation and promoted callosal neuron production. Further, we found that DACH1 is regulated by LHX2 via a primate-evolved enhancer. Introducing this enhancer into mice promoted bRG generation, while its removal in primates impaired bRG production.

Mechanistically, DACH1 promotes bRG generation by suppressing miR-215-5p–mediated down-regulation of centromere- and centrosome-related genes. These findings reveal a mechanism by which cortical progenitor expansion shapes the primate cortical connectome for cognitive evolution.

Latest Update: Why Viruses Make You Sneeze: COVID Proteins Directly Hijack Sensory Nerves

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (977 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Neuroscientists have discovered that SARS-CoV-2 viral proteins directly activate pain-sensing nerves in the airways to trigger sneezing, coughing, and body aches, overturning the long-held view that symptoms stem solely from immune inflammation.
  • The study demonstrates that the viral enzyme PLpro activates the wasabi-sensing TRPA1 receptor on sensory neurons, offering newly introduced therapeutic targets for acute viral symptoms and long COVID.
  • Sources indicate that for decades, textbooks have explained the misery of respiratory infections, the racking coughs, relentless sneezing, headaches, and full-body aches, as collateral damage from the immune system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Neuroscientists have discovered that SARS-CoV-2 viral proteins directly activate pain-sensing nerves in the airways to trigger sneezing, coughing, and body aches, overturning the long-held view that symptoms stem solely from immune inflammation.

The study demonstrates that the viral enzyme PLpro activates the wasabi-sensing TRPA1 receptor on sensory neurons, offering newly introduced therapeutic targets for acute viral symptoms and long COVID.

Sources indicate that for decades, textbooks have explained the misery of respiratory infections, the racking coughs, relentless sneezing, headaches, and full-body aches, as collateral damage from the immune system. According to conventional wisdom, infected airway cells and responding immune cells release a storm of inflammatory mediators that secondarily irritate nearby nerve endings.

Now, a study published in the journal Neuron reveals that coronaviruses do not wait for the immune system to sound the alarm; their viral proteins directly hijack the peripheral nervous system.

In a recent development, led by Dr. Diana Bautista, professor of molecular and cell biology at UC Berkeley, member of the Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute, and a Howard Hughes Medical Institute (HHMI) investigator, the research demonstrates that specific SARS-CoV-2 enzymes directly stimulate airway sensory neurons, triggering immediate sneezing, coughing, airway inflammation, and heightened pain sensitivity.

Recent findings suggest that when SARS-CoV-2 infects host cells, it manufactures two specialized enzymes, papain-like protease (PLpro) and main protease (Mpro), to slice long viral polyproteins into functional components needed for viral replication. Once the virus kills the host cell, these viral proteases spill into the surrounding airway tissue, coming into direct contact with specialized pain- and irritant-sensing neurons known as nociceptors.

Bautista, who previously discovered that the TRPA1 ion channel acts as the sensory receptor for pungent chemicals in wasabi and garlic, found that SARS-CoV-2 hijacks this exact molecular pathway:.

Sources indicate that to test how PLpro behaves in a living organism, Bautista’s team applied just two microliters of purified PLpro to the nostrils of mice. While plain water occasionally elicited a single sneeze, PLpro triggered explosive bouts of up to 30 sneezes per minute, alongside heightened mechanical pain sensitivity.

Sources indicate that convincing peer reviewers that mice genuinely sneeze required rigorous physiological proof. The team acquired a specialized $75,000 plethysmograph to record the characteristic respiratory lung spasms accompanying each sneeze, matching patterns documented in other sneezing mammals, and dyed the nasal fluid blue to measure the expelled aerosol volume.

While antiviral medications like Paxlovid target Mpro to halt viral replication, numerous experimental inhibitors targeting PLpro were developed during the pandemic without yet reaching clinical approval.

Sources indicate that “We think that these protease inhibitors that people spent a lot of time and money developing could be important not just for preventing viral replication,” noted Bautista. “They could also help treat symptoms like coughing, which could limit viral spread, and potentially prevent severe COVID-19 in individuals who are susceptible.”.

Furthermore, direct viral sensitization of nociceptors offers a compelling biological mechanism for chronic neurological and respiratory complaints in long COVID—including persistent cough, shortness of breath, chest pain, and headaches.

“There are many modes by which viral and bacterial infections can act in our bodies — there are distinct molecular and cellular routes of triggering this type of airway hyper-reactivity,” Bautista noted. “So far, it looks like they can drive symptoms through both the immune system and the nervous system, using different molecular mechanisms.”.

How does SARS-CoV-2 cause sneezing, coughing, and body aches so quickly?

Researchers discovered that when virus-infected cells die, they release viral enzymes, specifically papain-like protease (PLpro) and main protease (Mpro), that directly stimulate pain-sensing nerves (nociceptors) in the airways, triggering immediate sneezing, coughing, and pain rather than waiting solely for immune inflammation.

What is the TRPA1 receptor, and what does it have to do with COVID-19?

Recent findings suggest that TRPA1 is an ion channel on sensory nerves famously known as the “wasabi receptor” because it detects irritating chemicals in wasabi and garlic. The study found that SARS-CoV-2’s PLpro enzyme directly activates TRPA1 on airway nerves, causing the release of neuropeptides that trigger coughing, sneezing, and pain.

Could these findings lead to new treatments for COVID-19 or long COVID?

It has been revealed that yes. Blocking the PLpro enzyme with targeted protease inhibitors could calm overactive sensory nerves, helping to stop severe coughing, reduce airborne viral spread, and potentially alleviate chronic neuropathic symptoms like persistent cough, chest pain, and headaches seen in long COVID.

Recent findings suggest that funding: The work was funded by grants from the National Institutes of Health (OD TR01 NS116992) and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. Co-authors of the paper are Sonali Mali, Ricardo Silva, Zhongyan Gong, Michael Cronce, Uyen Vo, Cliff Vuong and Jeffery Cox of UC Berkeley and Yalda Moayedi of the New York University College of Dentistry. Bautista is a member of Berkeley’s Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute.

A coronavirus protease activates sensory neurons via TRPA1 to drive sneeze, cough, and pain.

In a recent development, sneezing, coughing, and pain are common symptoms of respiratory viral infection. These responses are initiated by airway-innervating nociceptors that detect noxious stimuli, but how SARS-CoV-2 activates these neurons remains unclear.

Here, we show that the coronavirus papain-like protease (PLpro) directly activates airway-innervating nociceptors in mice and human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived nociceptors. PLpro triggers sneezing, coughing, acute pain, and calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) release in the airways.

Both the proteolytic activity of PLpro and the host ion channel transient receptor potential ankyrin 1 (TRPA1) are required for neuronal activation and sneezing. Infection with the mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 or the murine coronavirus MHV-A59 also induces sneezing in mice, and MHV-A59-evoked sneezing is TRPA1-dependent. SARS-CoV-2 infection of the trigeminal ganglia altered transcriptional programs associated with nociception, including upregulation of the TRPA1-CGRP signaling pathway activated by PLpro.

Together, these findings reveal a direct mechanism by which SARS-CoV-2 triggers pain and airway reflexes and identify PLpro and TRPA1 as potential therapeutic targets for COVID-19.

Coffee doesn’t have to keep you awake to disrupt your sleep

📅 22 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (762 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that for years, people have debated whether drinking coffee in the evening interferes with sleep.
  • To investigate those effects, scientists are using EEG, or electroencephalography -- a method used to record the brain's electrical activity.
  • "EEG allows us to see not only whether a person is sleeping, but also how the brain is sleeping.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for years, people have debated whether drinking coffee in the evening interferes with sleep. Some people can have caffeine late in the day and fall asleep easily, while others may remain awake for hours. But researchers are increasingly finding that simply asking whether coffee delays sleep may miss a more vital glitch: what caffeine does to the brain after sleep begins.

To investigate those effects, scientists are using EEG, or electroencephalography -- a method used to record the brain's electrical activity. EEG measurements can reveal much more than how long someone sleeps or how often they wake up. They can also provide clues about the biological quality and depth of that sleep.

"EEG allows us to see not only whether a person is sleeping, but also how the brain is sleeping. Classical sleep assessment assesses sleep duration and its stages, whereas quantitative EEG analysis reveals more subtle changes, such as reduced slow-wave activity, which is an crucial marker of sleep depth and its restorative character," explains Prof. Donata Kurpas from the Department of Nursing, Wroclaw Medical University.

Slow waves are a major feature of deep sleep -- the stage associated with physical recovery, replenishing energy reserves, and maintaining healthy brain function.

Caffeine May Make Sleep Less Restorative.

Recent findings suggest that caffeine does not always affect sleep in obvious ways. A person may still fall asleep at a normal time and remain asleep for what appears to be a full night, yet the quality of that rest may still be altered.

In a recent development, "Caffeine may shorten sleep or make it more difficult to fall asleep; however, even when sleep duration appears normal, it may reduce slow-wave activity and shift the EEG pattern toward a more 'wakeful' brain," states Prof. Kurpas.

In practical terms, someone might spend eight hours in bed without getting the same level of neurological recovery they would normally expect. Because the disruption may not cause obvious awakenings, it can easily go unnoticed.

"The subjective feeling of having slept well does not always correspond to what we observe in neurophysiological recordings. A person may fall asleep without major difficulty and not remember awakenings, while the brain may display fewer features of deep sleep," the expert adds.

Why Caffeine Affects People Differently.

In a recent development, another major finding from caffeine research is that responses vary considerably from person to person. Genetics, metabolism, age, stress, and chronic fatigue can all influence how strongly caffeine affects sleep.

For some people, even coffee consumed early in the day may still have an impact by nighttime.

Recent findings suggest that "It is not only about coffee consumed just before bedtime. For some people, the total amount of caffeine consumed during the day and whether the body has enough time to metabolize it before nightfall may also be key," Prof. Kurpas emphasizes.

That possibility may be especially relevant for people who rely on caffeine to improve focus, stamina, or performance, including athletes, people doing mentally demanding work, and anyone who regularly uses coffee or other caffeinated products to stay alert.

Caffeine Can Create a Fatigue Cycle.

Caffeine can temporarily increase alertness and make fatigue feel less noticeable. However, experts caution that the boost may sometimes come at the expense of the body's ability to recover fully during sleep.

In that sense, caffeine can resemble "borrowing energy" from the body. If nighttime recovery becomes less effective, the person may feel more tired the following day and turn to even more caffeine for help.

In a recent development, "If caffeine helps a person function during the day while simultaneously worsening the quality of nighttime recovery, a vicious circle may develop: greater fatigue, greater need for stimulation, and poorer sleep," says Prof. Kurpas.

Recent findings suggest that these findings are one reason sleep researchers are paying less attention to sleep duration alone. Increasingly, the focus is shifting toward what the brain is actually doing during the night and whether that sleep is biologically restorative.

"Caffeine is neither 'good' nor 'bad'. It is a biologically active substance whose effects depend on dose, time of day, age, lifestyle, sleep quality, stress burden, and individual sensitivity," the expert concludes.
